title: Fine-Tuning Disentangled Context Memory for Video Editing with Flow-Based GRPO
abstract: Recent video editing models struggle to maintain object identity across multiple edits. PermaVid introduced a disentangled context memory to address this, yet the memory readout is not directly optimized for user instruction adherence. In this work, we propose an incremental extension that applies a flow-based GRPO objective to fine-tune the context memory readout of a frozen video diffusion backbone, rewarding edits that preserve identity while following editing instructions. To make the approach tractable, we use a lightweight reward model based on clip similarity and an instruction-following metric. We evaluate in a limited setting on a subset of the EditBench dataset with 100 prompts per task, and report initial results suggesting modest gains in identity preservation over the PermaVid baseline, but we do not measure full editing quality or compare against recent instruction-editing baselines due to compute constraints. We also omit ablations of the reward weighting and memory size. While the improvement is marginal and the evaluation incomplete, our preliminary findings indicate that reinforcement fine-tuning of memory modules is a promising direction, though substantial revision and broader benchmarking are required for any practical deployment.

title: Multi-Turn LLM Performance in Interactive Fiction Across EU Languages: A Preliminary Evaluation
abstract: Recent research has highlighted disparities in multi-turn LLM performance across languages, but the impact of these disparities on complex interactive tasks remains underexplored. We investigate the performance of several multilingual LLMs in text-based game environments, where agents must maintain coherent dialogue and follow narrative constraints over multiple turns. Extending a prior multi-turn evaluation framework developed for EU-24 languages (Author, 2026), we focus on a subset of five languages and two interactive fiction scenarios. We measure dialogue consistency and task completion rates, comparing three proprietary and two open-weight models. Initial results suggest that model rankings shift across languages and that even high-performing models exhibit inconsistent behavior in game contexts, such as losing track of inventory items or contradicting prior statements. However, our evaluation is limited to a small set of scenarios, a short dialogue history of at most eight turns, and we do not include fine-tuned or instruction-tuned variants of the open models. We also lack a human baseline and do not perform ablations. Despite these limitations, our findings point to the need for more nuanced, task-oriented evaluation of multilingual multi-turn capabilities. We release our prompts and scenario descriptions for future work.

title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Extension for Privacy Budget Allocation in Encrypted Range Queries over Mobile Clouds
abstract: Privacy-preserving range queries in mobile cloud environments face a fundamental trade-off between query accuracy and privacy budget consumption, especially under varying workload intensities. While existing works have applied heuristic or rule-based strategies to allocate privacy budgets, these methods fail to adapt to dynamic query arrival patterns. In this paper, we extend a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework, originally developed for scheduling in blockchain payment channel networks, to the problem of privacy budget allocation for encrypted range queries in mobile edge clouds. The proposed method, termed DRL-PRQ, models each query as a state feature and learns a policy that selects either a Laplace mechanism or a truncated Gaussian mechanism per query, under a cumulative budget constraint. We evaluate DRL-PRQ in a limited simulation setting using a synthetic Gaussian dataset and a single query workload trace. Compared with a fixed-budget baseline, our initial results suggest that DRL-PRQ can reduce average query latency by approximately 12% while maintaining comparable privacy loss, though the improvement is not consistent across all privacy parameter regimes. We do not evaluate against other learning-based baselines or real-world datasets, and the reward shaping requires further tuning. Overall, this is a marginal and preliminary step toward adaptive privacy-aware query processing, requiring substantial revision and more comprehensive benchmarking.

title: Initializing Graph Neural Recommenders with Multi-Hop Knowledge Graph Embeddings: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Recent work has shown that incorporating knowledge graphs into recommender systems can alleviate data sparsity and improve interpretability. In this paper, we propose a simple extension to an existing graph neural network (GNN) based recommender by initializing user and item embeddings with pre-trained multi-hop knowledge graph representations. Specifically, we take entity embeddings obtained from a multi-hop reasoning model over a knowledge graph and use them as initial node features in a light graph convolution network. We then apply a lightweight attention mechanism to aggregate neighborhood information during propagation. We evaluate our approach in a limited setting on two public datasets, comparing only against a single baseline due to computational constraints. Initial results suggest that the proposed initialization yields modest improvements in Recall@20 and NDCG@20 over the baseline, but the gains are not consistent across all item categories. We do not include a full ablation study of the attention component or a sensitivity analysis of hyperparameters, and we acknowledge that a more comprehensive evaluation against state-of-the-art methods is required. Overall, our findings indicate that this direction is promising but requires further investigation to fully validate its effectiveness.

title: DiffPatch: Distributional Location-Aware Adversarial Patches for Robust World Models
abstract: We present DiffPatch, a new generative framework for distributional adversarial patch robustness in vision-based world models. Unlike prior patch attacks that optimize a single appearance at a fixed location, DiffPatch learns a conditional diffusion model over the joint space of patch appearance and placement, allowing continuous-scale, physically realizable adversarial patches to be synthesized at any position. We formulate a new minimax training objective that couples the denoising network with a world model's perception encoder, and we solve it via a differentiable alternating update. This joint training enables the world model to defend against a distribution of patch attacks rather than a single one. On the nuScenes and KITTI future-prediction benchmarks, DiffPatch improves state-of-the-art robust accuracy from 62.3% to 68.7% and from 57.1% to 63.4%, respectively, under a 2% patch-area budget. On the CARLA autonomous-driving benchmark, the resulting world model raises end-to-end driving success from 71.5% to 78.2% and reduces collision rate by 31%. The gains are consistent across unseen patch scales, locations, and illuminations, confirming that DiffPatch learns a genuinely robust and generalizable patch distribution.

title: LinguaTurn: A Multi-Turn Multilingual Benchmark and Counterfactual Turn-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Robust Instruction Following
abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance on single-turn instruction following, their accuracy degrades substantially in multi-turn conversations, particularly for lower-resourced European languages. We introduce LinguaTurn, a new benchmark containing 10,000 multi-turn dialogues with instructions and reference responses, covering 24 EU languages and 4 language families. LinguaTurn comes with turn-level metrics for coherence and consistency, enabling fine-grained comparisons. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary LLMs (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, Gemma-7B, GPT-4, Claude-3.5, and GPT-3.5) and find that performance drops by an average of 11.7% between single-turn and fifth-turn instructions, with the largest drops for Estonian and Maltese. To address this, we propose Counterfactual Turn-Augmented Fine-tuning (CTAF), a data-curation strategy that reorders, inserts distractors, and removes turns to make models robust to dialogue dynamics. On LinguaTurn, CTAF improves accuracy by 4.2 points over standard fine-tuning and by 6.1 points over zero-shot prompting, with negligible cost on standard single-turn benchmarks. Human evaluation on a 200-dialogue subset confirms that CTAF outputs are more coherent and consistent. We release code and data.

title: Language-Modulated Overfitting Control in Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Deep offline reinforcement learning (RL) is often prone to overfitting to the static dataset, particularly when the training environment is narrow. Recent work has shown that regulating overfitting significantly improves online deep RL, but less is known about whether the same regularization transfers to the offline setting. In this paper, we investigate a straightforward extension: adding dropout and weight decay to an offline RL algorithm while augmenting its reward signal with auxiliary semantic rewards generated by a pretrained language model. We combine these two ingredients in a single framework and evaluate on a limited set of tasks from the D4RL benchmark, using only the medium-expert and medium datasets for two locomotion environments. In our experiments, the proposed regularization improves normalized score on half of the tested datasets, while on the other half it slightly degrades performance relative to a standard CQL baseline. We also ablate the language-model reward component alone and find inconsistent gains. We report a complementary analysis of the learned Q-values to provide initial evidence about the interaction between the two components. These initial results are mixed but suggest that language-modulated overfitting control may help in offline RL when the dataset is narrow, but not across the board. We believe substantial further tuning and larger-scale evaluation are necessary before drawing stronger conclusions.

title: Applying Deep Temporal Graph Learning to Fake News Propagation: A Preliminary Study on a Small Twitter Dataset
abstract: We present a preliminary application of deep temporal graph learning to the task of fake news propagation modeling. Specifically, we apply a structural embedding pre-trained temporal graph network, originally developed for general dynamic graph forecasting, to the spread of misinformation on social media. Our goal is to explore whether this existing method can capture the temporal dynamics of fake news cascades when adapted with minimal changes. We use a single, small dataset of 500 manually annotated fake news propagation trees extracted from Twitter, covering a two-week period. In our initial experiments, we train the model to predict the next node in the cascade and report accuracy and F1 scores on a held-out test set. We do not compare against any baselines, as the focus is on feasibility rather than superiority. The results show moderate performance, indicating that the approach may have some potential but requires substantial further investigation. We explicitly acknowledge the limitations: the dataset is very small, there is no benchmarking against state-of-the-art methods, and the model is applied off-the-shelf without any domain-specific adaptation. Consequently, our findings are only suggestive and should be interpreted with caution.

title: Latency-Aware Scheduling for Geometry-Grounded Track-Anything Models in Streaming Video
abstract: We present an incremental extension of the G2TAM framework by coupling it with a latency-aware scheduling heuristic originally designed for streaming 3D perception. The core contribution is a geometric-displacement gate that decides when to run the tracking model, reducing inference frequency while preserving object identity in video. This combines existing ideas from geometry grounding and latency-aware perception into a single pipeline. We evaluate in a limited setting: one video sequence from MMSI-Video-Bench, two object categories, and we compare against a single baseline (fixed-frame-rate G2TAM). We do not perform ablations on the gate threshold, nor do we test on other benchmarks. Initial results suggest that the proposed gate reduces model invocations by ~20% with only a minor decrease in association accuracy in this specific scenario. These are preliminary findings; the gain is modest and may not generalize to cluttered scenes or higher-speed egomotion. We believe the idea is interesting but requires substantial revision, more thorough evaluation, and an expanded ablation study before any stronger claim can be made.

title: Applying Structured Chain-of-Thought Prompting to Quantum Circuit Code Generation: Initial Experiments
abstract: We apply structured chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, previously proposed for general-purpose code generation, to the new domain of quantum circuit code generation. The method is used exactly as originally described, with no adaptation or methodological novelty. We explore whether its staged decomposition—requirement analysis, algorithm planning, and code synthesis—transfers from imperative Python code to the gate-based, declarative style of Qiskit programs. In initial experiments on a single author-collected dataset of 80 natural-language-to-quantum-circuit problems, we use one large language model (GPT-4) and report raw generation outcomes. The structured prompt yields syntactically valid Qiskit code in most cases, but functional correctness, measured by matching reference circuit outputs, is low and highly variable across problem types. We do not compare against other prompting methods, do not test multiple models, and do not ablate any components. The dataset is small, domain-specific, and created by the authors, so results may not generalize. These preliminary findings indicate that structured CoT offers only limited benefit for this domain, warranting further study with larger datasets and stronger evaluation.

title: Batch-Aware Contrastive Fine-Tuning of Universal Cell Embeddings with Dynamic Hard Negative Mining
abstract: Universal cell embeddings are foundation models that encode single-cell RNA-seq profiles into a shared latent space, enabling transfer across datasets and tissues. However, their generalization is limited by residual batch effects and the difficulty of learning discriminative features for rare cell types. We introduce CellAlign, a self-supervised contrastive fine-tuning method that adapts a pre-trained universal embedding model to a noisy target corpus while preserving its broad prior knowledge. CellAlign constructs positive pairs via reciprocal k-nearest neighbors in the embedding space and uses a dynamic hard negative mining strategy that prioritizes in-batch negatives that are close in the embedding but distinct in the observed expression program. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, we add a regularization term that anchors the fine-tuned model to the original embedding function. We evaluate CellAlign on six publicly available single-cell datasets spanning diverse tissues and sequencing protocols, benchmarking against the frozen foundation model, scVI, and a vanilla contrastive fine-tuning baseline. CellAlign improves average cell-type classification F1 by 11.3% and batch-integration metrics (kBET and ARI) by a large margin, with largest gains on rare populations. While the method requires a representative target dataset for fine-tuning and incurs moderate compute overhead, it consistently outperforms baselines even with as few as 10,000 cells. Our results demonstrate that targeted contrastive fine-tuning is a practical, low-resource pathway to adapt universal cell embeddings to domain-specific single-cell atlases.

title: Latent Entity Anchors for In-Context Knowledge Graph Completion: Initial Results with Code World Models
abstract: Knowledge graph foundation models (KGFMs) such as KGPFN have shown that in-context learning can adapt to unseen graph schemas. However, their performance degrades when entity labels are sparse or semantically ambiguous, because the model must infer entity identity solely from the prompt. In this paper we combine two existing ideas: we inject latent entity anchors extracted from a code world model (VisualPatchWorld-style patch encodings) into the in-context exemplars of KGPFN. The anchors are generated offline by a pretrained patch transformer and appended as structured tokens to each example, rather than training a new architecture. This is an incremental extension of prior work, not a new method. We evaluate on two subsets of Wikidata5M and a small biomedical triple set, measuring Hits@10 and MRR. Our initial results suggest that anchor injection yields modest gains on entities with patch-correlated images, while performance on text-only entities is unchanged. We do not compare against full KGPFN baselines with larger context windows, and we omit ablation of the anchor dimension and injection position. In this limited setting, we cannot yet determine whether the gains are due to the anchors or to the increased prompt length. Overall, the contribution is marginal and needs substantial revision.

title: SignAlign: Language-Guided Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning for Isolated Sign Language Recognition
abstract: We propose SignAlign, a novel contrastive learning framework for isolated sign language recognition that jointly aligns pose keypoint sequences and RGB frames with textual gloss embeddings from a pre-trained language model. The core contribution is a pose-aware attention module that learns to weight each keypoint by its linguistic salience, guided by a distillation objective from a multi-modal model, thereby reducing noise from irrelevant body movements. To further mitigate modality bias, we introduce a cross-modal consistency regularizer that aligns classifier predictions across pose and RGB streams, and combine it with a masked temporal contrastive loss for robust representation learning. On the WLASL100 and MSASL100 benchmarks, SignAlign achieves 82.4% and 85.1% top-1 accuracy, outperforming recent sign recognition baselines by 3.2 and 2.7 percentage points, respectively. Using only 5% of labeled training data, our semi-supervised variant surpasses fully supervised baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of leveraging language priors. We also analyze failure cases involving signs with high handshape variation, which points to limitations in current keypoint representations. Code and models will be released publicly.

title: Watermarking Multilingual ASR Transcripts: An Initial Extension of TextSeal to Speech Recognition Outputs
abstract: We propose a lightweight extension of TextSeal, a localized LLM watermarking scheme, to the outputs of multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. The goal is to embed provenance markers directly into ASR transcripts so that synthetic or machine-generated text can be traced back to its source model. Our approach adapts the token-level watermarking mechanism of TextSeal to operate on ASR hypotheses, exploiting the fact that ASR decoders typically produce token sequences over a fixed vocabulary. We apply the watermark during beam search by biasing the selection of tokens that carry a secret key, similar to the original TextSeal formulation. We evaluate on transcripts from two multilingual ASR systems (faster-whisper and a small fine-tuned wav2vec2.0 model) for four languages (English, French, Hindi, and Swahili) from the Common Voice corpus. Results show that watermark detection remains robust for English and French, but degradation occurs for lower-resource languages due to higher word error rates and tokenization mismatches. We also observe a slight increase in word error rate (average +0.8%) when the watermark is enabled. Our study is limited to a single dataset and two ASR models; we do not evaluate against stronger paraphrasing attacks or test on streaming ASR. Initial results suggest that TextSeal-based watermarking can be transferred to ASR transcripts with modest cost, but more work is needed to handle multilingual tokenization and to preserve quality in low-resource settings.

title: Applying Function-Space Variational Inference to Uncertainty-Aware Bank Term Deposit Prediction: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Function-space variational inference (FSVI) is a recent approach for uncertainty estimation in Bayesian neural networks that directly matches a variational distribution in function space. In this paper, we apply FSVI to the problem of predicting bank term deposit subscriptions from telemarketing call data. We use the UCI Bank Marketing dataset, from which we randomly select a subset of 5,000 instances to keep computational costs manageable. We train a Bayesian neural network with a Gaussian process prior in function space using the FSVI objective and report classification accuracy, AUC, and expected calibration error. Our initial experiments show that FSVI can be trained on this small dataset and achieves reasonable performance in terms of accuracy (around 0.86) and calibration (ECE around 0.05). However, we do not compare against other uncertainty estimation methods or even a standard neural network baseline, so the practical benefits of FSVI in this domain remain unclear. We also note that the dataset is heavily imbalanced and our subset may not be representative. These preliminary results are intended to explore the feasibility of applying FSVI beyond the synthetic benchmarks in the original work; we make no claims of state-of-the-art performance.

title: Grounded Latent World Models: Evidence-Constrained State Abstractions for Knowledge-Consistent Planning
abstract: World models that plan in learned latent spaces are prone to hallucinated transitions—latent states that are not entailed by observed evidence. We formalize this failure as the problem of grounded latent consistency, and propose GLOW (Grounded Latent Optimization with World-knowledge), a novel framework that couples a latent world model with a knowledge-graph foundation model and an agentic entailment verifier. At each planning step, GLOW performs differentiable optimization over the latent code, simultaneously minimizing transition prediction error and maximizing entailment probability with respect to retrieved evidence paths from the knowledge graph. To evaluate this setting we introduce WorldPlanBench, a new benchmark of 2,000 long-horizon plan generation tasks in four domains, each paired with gold knowledge evidence. GLOW sets state-of-the-art results: plan success climbs from 41.3% to 68.9% on WorldPlanBench, from 25.6% to 47.3% on ALFWorld, and 0.93 plan executability (vs 0.71 for the strongest prior) on VirtualHome. Importantly, GLOW cuts hallucinated state entities by 74.2% relative to the strongest latent world model baseline on our state-consistency metric, and improves downstream task reward by 22.4% on average across all benchmarks. These results demonstrate that explicit evidence grounding of latent state abstractions is necessary and feasible for reliable world-model planning.

title: Zero-Shot Isolated Sign Language Recognition with CLIP: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We explore the application of a pre-trained vision-language model, CLIP, to isolated sign language recognition. Our method treats each sign language video as a sequence of static frames, extracts frame-level features using CLIP's image encoder, and classifies via cosine similarity with text embeddings of gloss labels. No fine-tuning, architectural modification, or temporal modeling is employed. We conduct initial experiments on a small subset of the MSASL dataset, consisting of 20 sign classes and 500 videos. Preliminary results indicate that this straightforward application achieves a top-1 accuracy of approximately 18%, which is substantially lower than specialized sign language models reported in the literature. However, we note that no baseline comparisons are included in this study. The primary limitations are the absence of temporal information, the reliance on frame sampling, the restricted vocabulary size, and the lack of hyperparameter tuning. We position this work as an initial exploration to assess the feasibility of directly using general-purpose vision-language models for sign language understanding, and we highlight open challenges for future research.

title: Language-Adaptive Denoising Pre-training for Multilingual Machine Translation
abstract: Multilingual denoising pre-training has become a standard recipe for neural machine translation, but existing methods apply a uniform corruption strategy to all languages during pre-training. In this paper, we identify that uniformly sampled span masking is suboptimal for multilingual translation because it fails to account for differences in token frequency, morphological complexity, and data availability across languages. We propose LanAdapt-Corrupt, a language-adaptive denoising objective that adjusts span length and masking rate per language during pre-training. The schedule is derived from a small, cheap set of language-family statistics, namely the average token length, morphological productivity, and corpus size; low-resource and highly inflectional languages use shorter, less aggressive corruption to preserve surface forms that are difficult to reconstruct. To facilitate transfer, we also introduce a shared corruption-policy network that predicts span lengths from language embeddings and is trained jointly with the denoiser. We pre-train a model on 25 languages and evaluate it on the WMT-9 and TED-8 many-to-many translation benchmarks. Our model outperforms random-span denoising baselines, including mBART, by +1.8 BLEU on average, and improves low-resource translation by up to +3.1 BLEU. In addition, it remains competitive on high-resource pairs. Ablations confirm that both the language-adaptive schedule and the policy network contribute to the gain. A limitation is that the schedule depends on coarse language-family typology and may not generalize to dialectal variation; we leave fine-grained adaptation for future work.

title: Applying Adaptive Federated Averaging to Wearable Stress Detection: Initial Experiments and Preliminary Results
abstract: We apply adaptive federated averaging (FedAvg with per-client learning rates) to the task of stress detection from wearable sensor data. This is a direct application of an existing method to a new domain, and we do not propose any algorithmic modifications. We explore whether adaptive per-client step sizes can improve convergence and accuracy in a federated setting where user data is distributed across devices and cannot be shared due to privacy constraints. We run initial experiments on a small public dataset of 12 participants with a simple feedforward network and a fixed number of communication rounds. Our preliminary results show that adaptive federated averaging reaches a higher test accuracy than standard FedAvg after 50 rounds in a single train/test split. However, this work has several clear limitations: the dataset is small and homogeneous, we do not compare against any other federated optimization methods or centralized baselines, and we do not perform any hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, the privacy analysis is limited to the use of federated averaging without any formal differential privacy guarantees. These results should be viewed as an early exploration rather than a conclusive evaluation.

title: Role-Conditioned Advantage Estimation for Cooperative Policy Learning in Imperfect-Information Tabletop Games
abstract: We introduce Role-Conditioned Advantage Estimation (RCAE), a novel policy-gradient method for training cooperative agents in multiplayer tabletop games with imperfect information. RCAE decomposes the shared team reward into role-specific advantage estimates using a mixed-motive potential function, allowing a single policy network to simultaneously optimize distinct agent roles (e.g., leader, supporter, or scout) while preserving joint coordination. The method requires no additional domain knowledge beyond a role assignment, making it applicable to a range of cooperative tabletop settings. We evaluate RCAE on two benchmark environments: a cooperative variant of Hanabi with four roles and a hidden-traitor tabletop game with asymmetric objectives. We compare against standard PPO, independent PPO, and a state-of-the-art opponent-modeling baseline. Results show that RCAE achieves statistically significant improvements in team win rate by 9.2% in Hanabi and 11.7% in the hidden-traitor game, while also producing more interpretable and behaviorally distinct role profiles, as measured by a behavioral embedding analysis. We further ablate the contribution of the potential function and show that RCAE is robust to varying team compositions. Minor limitations include a fixed role assignment during training and increased computational cost for the advantage estimator. Overall, RCAE offers a practical and effective framework for role-aware multi-agent training in imperfect-information games.

title: Zero-Shot Grounded Cells: A Preliminary Study of Grounded SAM for Nuclei Segmentation in Histopathology Images
abstract: Recent open-world vision models such as Grounded SAM combine grounding and segmentation capabilities, allowing users to prompt with free-form text. In this paper, we investigate a straightforward extension: using Grounded SAM in a zero-shot manner to segment cell nuclei from H&E-stained histopathology images. We prompt the model with descriptive texts such as 'nucleus' and 'cell' and evaluate on a subset of the public PanNuke dataset containing 250 images. Our initial results show that while the model can localize some nuclei, the segmentation quality is brittle—varying with prompt phrasing and image stain color—and the average Dice score (0.32) is considerably lower than the supervised U-Net baseline (0.71). We do not fine-tune or adapt the model, and we did not have the resources to run ablations on prompt templates or to compare across additional datasets. We also observe that combining multiple prompt terms can sometimes confuse the grounding module, resulting in false positives on non-nucleus structures. Our limited experiments suggest that direct zero-shot application of open-world grounding models to histopathology is not yet competitive, but the ability to interactively prompt may still offer a useful starting point for annotation. We release our evaluation code and prompt templates to facilitate reproducibility.

title: Conformal Relevance Labeling for Black-box Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We propose Conformal Relevance Labeling (CRL), an extension of the ARL2 framework for aligning retrievers with black-box large language models (LLMs). ARL2 uses self-guided adaptive relevance labeling to train retrieval models without access to LLM internals, but produces only point-wise relevance scores without uncertainty estimates. CRL adds a conformal prediction layer to output calibrated confidence sets over retrieved passages, enabling the LLM to abstain or expand its retrieval set when uncertainty is high. We evaluate CRL on two open-domain QA benchmarks (Natural Questions and TriviaQA) using a fixed black-box LLM (GPT-3.5) and a bi-encoder retriever. In this limited setting, CRL yields modest gains over ARL2 in answer recall and expected calibration error, and the conformal sets are often small yet informative. However, we do not compare against other uncertainty-aware retrieval methods, nor do we ablate the effects of calibration set size or self-guided labeling iterations. Initial results suggest that conformal prediction can provide a useful uncertainty signal for black-box RAG, though improvements on TriviaQA fall within noise range. Overall, the contribution is incremental, combining two existing ideas with preliminary evidence that warrants further investigation.

title: Applying a Blockchain-Based Reputation Mechanism to Federated Learning for Heart Disease Prediction: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We apply an existing blockchain-based reputation aggregation mechanism, originally designed for collaborative spectrum sensing, to the domain of cross-silo federated learning for heart disease prediction. The mechanism maintains a decentralized reputation score for each participating client and uses it to weight model updates during aggregation. We implement this approach on top of standard FedAvg and simulate a federated environment using the UCI Heart Disease dataset, partitioned across five clients to mimic different hospital data distributions. In initial experiments, the reputation mechanism successfully mitigates the impact of a single label-flipping adversary, with accuracy degradation reduced compared to naive averaging. However, this preliminary work has major limitations. The evaluation is restricted to a single small dataset with a binary classification task, and no baseline comparisons are made against established robust aggregation methods such as Krum, Trimmed Mean, or coordinate-wise median. The threat model considers only one attack type, the client population is fixed, and blockchain parameters are taken directly from the original protocol without tuning. As an early exploratory study, our findings should be interpreted with caution; extensive validation on larger, more heterogeneous datasets and a broader set of adversarial scenarios is necessary before drawing any practical conclusions.

title: Applying Structure-Adaptive Multi-View Graph Clustering to Multispectral Drone Imagery: Preliminary Results
abstract: Multi-view graph clustering has shown promising results for remote sensing image analysis. In this paper, we apply a state-of-the-art structure-adaptive multi-view graph clustering method, originally developed for satellite remote sensing, to a new domain: multispectral drone imagery of agricultural crop fields. This is a direct application with no methodological novelty; we reuse the original algorithm and its default parameters. We conduct initial experiments on a single small dataset comprising 120 drone images collected from one farm. No baseline comparisons are performed, and we do not tune any hyperparameters. The preliminary results indicate a clustering accuracy of only 61.8% on our dataset, which is substantially lower than typical results reported for the original domain. Visual inspection of the clusters shows poor separation between crop types and many fragmented clusters. These findings suggest that the existing algorithm does not transfer well without domain-specific adaptations. We explicitly acknowledge the limitations of this work, including the small dataset size, the lack of comparison, and the single-run evaluation. We consider this a preliminary exploration rather than a comprehensive study. Future work will involve larger datasets, hyperparameter tuning, and comparisons with existing clustering baselines.

title: A Preliminary Study on Region-Level Visual Reward Modeling for Referring Expression Comprehension
abstract: Recent progress in multimodal reward models has shown promise for aligning vision-language models with human preferences. In this work, we present a straightforward extension of the Unified Reward Model (URM) to region-level visual preference scoring for referring expression comprehension. Our approach combines URM's existing global scoring capability with a visual equivalence signal computed from cropped image regions, following the idea of Visual-ERM. We construct preference pairs from the RefCOCOg dataset and fine-tune URM using a margin ranking loss. In a limited evaluation, we compare our model against URM and a random baseline on the validation set, reporting only accuracy on the held-out split. Initial results suggest that the region-aware reward model provides a slight improvement in preference ranking accuracy over the baseline, but the gain is not consistent across all categories. Due to compute constraints, we do not perform ablations on the equivalence signal or cross-dataset generalization. These preliminary findings indicate that while region-level reward modeling is a plausible direction, substantial refinement and additional evaluation are required before the approach can be considered practical. We discuss potential limitations and future work.

title: Applying Fine-tuned Qwen-7B to Cross-Lingual Entity Alignment in Historical Chinese Local Gazetteers: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We apply a fine-tuned Qwen-7B model to the task of cross-lingual entity alignment between historical Chinese local gazetteers and a modern geographic knowledge base. The task requires linking person and place names in classical Chinese text to English-language entries in Wikidata, which is challenging due to historical naming conventions and sparse contextual clues. Our approach is a straightforward application of an existing seq2seq fine-tuning recipe: we treat alignment as a generation problem and train Qwen-7B on a small corpus of 120 manually aligned gazetteer excerpts. We report preliminary results on a held-out set of 30 excerpts, achieving an accuracy of 0.62 for place entities and 0.41 for person entities. We do not compare against baselines, as the dataset is built solely for this study and no prior work has directly addressed this exact setting. We acknowledge clear limitations: the dataset is very small and skews toward well-known localities, no error analysis is provided, and the fine-tuning procedure is borrowed without modification from prior work. These initial experiments suggest that large language models can assist human indexers, but the results are far from production-ready and require substantial further research.

title: Sparse Embedding Modulation for Chain-of-Thought Spatial Reasoning in Frozen Vision-Language Models: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Sparse Embedding Modulation (SEM) was recently introduced as a post-hoc debiasing method for vision-language models (VLMs) by selectively modulating a small subset of embedding dimensions. In this work, we extend SEM to the task of chain-of-thought (CoT) spatial reasoning for single-view 3D scene understanding. We apply SEM to a frozen VLM that is prompted to describe the layout of objects in a single RGB image and then answer questions about their relative positions. Our hypothesis is that SEM can reduce the object-attribute biases that often cause VLMs to produce implausible spatial relations. We evaluate our approach on a small subset of the ScanNet dataset, restricted to three object categories, and compare against two baselines: the unmodified VLM and a random modulation variant. Initial results suggest that SEM yields a slight improvement in answer accuracy (+2.3%) and produces more geometrically consistent CoT explanations. However, the gains are inconsistent across object pairs, and we do not perform ablations on the sparse modulation rate or compare to full fine-tuning or recent debiasing methods such as prompt tuning. These limitations make the findings preliminary; substantial further evaluation is required to establish the effectiveness of SEM for spatial reasoning.

title: Multi-Hop Knowledge Graph Reasoning for Session-Based Recommendation: An Incremental Extension and Preliminary Evaluation
abstract: Multi-hop knowledge graph reasoning has shown promise for interpretable link prediction, yet its application to recommendation has been mostly limited to static settings. In this paper, we extend a recently proposed few-shot knowledge graph reasoning framework to session-based recommendation by treating user-item interactions as entity-relation paths. Our approach adapts the reasoning module to incorporate session context and produces path-based explanations for recommended items. We evaluate the method on two public datasets, comparing against a single baseline and a non-reasoning variant. Initial results suggest that the proposed extension can improve recommendation accuracy and provide more interpretable path explanations, but the gains are inconsistent across settings and the path explanations occasionally contain irrelevant entities. Due to time and computational constraints, we do not perform extensive hyperparameter tuning, ablation studies, or comparison with state-of-the-art sequential recommenders. The evaluation is limited to offline accuracy metrics and a small qualitative analysis of path quality. Overall, this is a preliminary study indicating that adapting multi-hop reasoning to session-based recommendation is feasible, though substantial further work is required to establish robust improvements.

title: Semi-Supervised Referring Image Segmentation via Vision-Language Pseudo-Labeling and Prompt-Based Refinement
abstract: Recent work has shown that large vision-language models can serve as effective teachers for dense prediction tasks. In this paper, we explore a semi-supervised setting for referring image segmentation, where only a small set of image-region-text pairs is labeled and a large corpus of unlabeled images is available. We propose a simple framework that extends existing referring segmentation models (e.g., PolyFormer) by generating pseudo masks from a frozen vision-language model and then refining them with a prompt-aware student network. Our method also incorporates task explanation prompts to guide the student model across different referring expressions. We evaluate on the RefCOCO dataset with only 10% labeled data and compare against fully supervised baselines. Initial results suggest that our method improves over a strong self-training baseline by 2.3% IoU, but the gap to fully supervised remains large. We also observe that pseudo-label noise severely limits performance on harder expressions. Due to time constraints, we only report results on RefCOCO and do not include ablations on prompt designs or comparisons with other semi-supervised methods. Overall, our work presents a preliminary step toward reducing annotation cost for referring segmentation, though substantial improvements are needed.

title: Zero-Shot Entity Typing in 19th-Century Encyclopedia Snippets Using a Pre-trained Cross-Encoder: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Zero-shot entity typing in historical encyclopedia snippets is important for digital humanities. We apply a pre-trained cross-encoder model, originally designed for fine-grained entity typing in modern news text, to a new domain: a single small dataset of 200 snippets from a 19th-century encyclopedia. The method is used off-the-shelf with no fine-tuning, no prompt engineering, and no task-specific modifications. We explore its zero-shot performance by mapping the model's 125-type taxonomy to three coarse types (Person, Location, Organization). Initial experiments show a macro-F1 of 0.61 on this one dataset, with no baseline comparisons or ablation studies. We explicitly acknowledge that the dataset is very small, contains annotation noise, and the taxonomy mismatch leads to frequent misclassifications. Nested mentions are not handled, and the model's performance on rare types is poor. These preliminary results are insufficient to support any general claim. This paper presents a straightforward application of an existing model to a new domain, and no methodological novelty is claimed.

title: Exploring Hallucinated Claims in Python Question Answering: A Preliminary Application of the FACTOR Framework
abstract: Recent work has shown that evaluating large language models for accuracy can inadvertently incentivize hallucinated outputs. We apply the FACTOR hallucination evaluation framework, originally developed for open-domain question answering, to a new domain: technical question answering about the Python programming language. Our dataset consists of 120 manually collected Stack Overflow questions and corresponding answers generated by a fine-tuned LLaMA-2 model. Using the FACTOR prompt, we measure the proportion of answers containing unsupported claims. Initial experiments suggest that accuracy-based scoring indeed encourages the model to produce statements not entailed by the provided context, replicating prior findings in this new setting. However, these preliminary results are based on a single small dataset, and we do not compare against any baseline methods or alternative evaluation metrics. The lack of baselines, limited dataset size, and absence of statistical testing mean our conclusions are only suggestive. We explore this setting as a first step, and we explicitly acknowledge that broader claims about model behavior would require substantially larger and more diverse evaluation sets, multiple random seeds, and significance testing. This work is intended as a preliminary exploration only.

title: Follower-Guided Rollout Policies for Monte Carlo Tree Search in Cooperative Tabletop Games
abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is widely used in tabletop game agents, but cooperative domains remain difficult because the search must align individual actions with team goals. In this paper, we adapt the following-the-leader heuristic, originally developed for competitive multiplayer tabletop games, to cooperative settings and combine it with MCTS by using a lightweight leader-follower policy to bias rollouts. The leader is selected by a hand-crafted ranking over state features, and all other agents imitate the leader's chosen action during the rollout phase. We evaluate this approach in a limited setting: a single scenario of a cooperative tabletop game with three agents and a fixed initial state. Initial results suggest that follower-guided rollouts improve the win rate over random-rollout MCTS by a small margin, although the gain is not consistent across seeds and disappears when the leader ranking is inaccurate. Because the game environment was modified after a reinforcement learning baseline had been trained, we were unable to include that baseline, and we did not run ablations on rollout count or leader definition. These preliminary findings indicate that the proposed method can modestly help MCTS in cooperative tabletop games, but the contribution remains marginal and would need substantial revision before general claims are justified.

title: Applying a Pretrained Denoising Diffusion Spatio-Spectral Model to Hyperspectral Image Super-Resolution: Initial Experiments on a Single Urban Scene
abstract: We apply a pretrained denoising diffusion spatio-spectral model to hyperspectral image super-resolution. The model, originally designed for restoration, is transferred as-is to enhance the spatial resolution of a single small hyperspectral image of an urban scene, without any adjustment or fine-tuning. We explore the influence of the number of diffusion steps and the noise scaling factor on the output quality. Initial experiments, based only on this one dataset, yield qualitative and quantitative results in terms of PSNR, SSIM, and SAM. However, we report no comparison with existing super-resolution approaches, and the evaluation is limited to a single scene. The lack of baselines, the small scale of the data, and the absence of a careful sensitivity analysis constitute clear limitations. These outcomes should therefore be interpreted as preliminary and exploratory, rather than as evidence of effectiveness. We conclude that transferring the model to a new task and domain requires substantially more validation before any claim of practical utility is possible.

title: Grammar-Guided Modular Decoding for Structurally Constrained Generation in Low-Resource Languages
abstract: We present a modular decoding framework that imposes formal grammatical constraints on pretrained language models without fine-tuning. Targeted at low-resource languages where large-scale treebanks are unavailable, our method induces a lightweight context-free grammar from a small set of seed sentences (as little as 500 tokens) and uses it to prune the search space during beam search. This grammar acts as a separate control module, complementing the neural model's distribution, and can be swapped for different languages without retraining. We evaluate on two structurally distinct tasks: multilingual summarization (WikiLingua) and morphological inflection (UniMorph) covering 8 under-resourced languages. Compared with standard beam search, unconstrained sampling, and a lexical constrained decoding baseline (PD), our method improves grammatical acceptability by 6.5 points and BLEU by 2.1 points on average, while maintaining comparable lexical diversity. The gains are most pronounced for verb-final languages with rich case marking. Limitations remain: the induced grammars are approximations, and coverage on highly synthetic languages is incomplete. Nonetheless, our results demonstrate that syntactic control can be effectively factored out of the neural model, offering a path toward more controllable generation for low-resource languages.

title: Robust Federated Aggregation via Mutual Information-Based Trust and Decentralized Reputation Management
abstract: This paper presents FL-TRUST, a robust aggregation framework for federated learning (FL) that mitigates Byzantine and free-riding attacks using an information-theoretic trust score combined with blockchain-anchored reputation. In each round, FL-TRUST computes the mutual information between each client's gradient update and the global model to quantify the client's contribution and identify statistically anomalous updates. These trust scores are aggregated into a decentralized reputation ledger maintained via a lightweight blockchain protocol, enabling traceable and tamper-evident client history across rounds and tasks. The aggregation rule weighs client updates by a combination of instantaneous trust and historical reputation, effectively down-weighting malicious or lazy participants. We evaluate FL-TRUST on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 under various attack scenarios, including label flipping, random gradient, and free-riding. Compared to standard FedAvg, Krum, and Trimmed Mean, FL-TRUST reduces model accuracy degradation by up to 60% under a 30% Byzantine clients and converges up to 2x faster in non-IID settings. We also analyze the communication and computational overhead of the blockchain component, which remains modest for moderate client counts. A limitation is that the method assumes a bounded fraction of malicious participants and relies on the initial global model to be benign. Overall, FL-TRUST provides a practical and interpretable defense for decentralized FL.

title: Adding Template-Based Explanations to a Conversational Critiquing System: Initial Results from a Small User Study
abstract: Conversational recommender systems have shown promise for eliciting user preferences through natural language. Building on prior work on attribute-aware item-set recommendations, this paper presents an incremental extension that combines a pre-existing conversational agent with template-based explanations for critiquing. Our approach reuses the conversational flow from earlier work and augments it with a simple explanation generation module that paraphrases the system's current attribute preferences. To assess this integration, we conduct a small user study (N=14) in a limited domain with a single dataset, comparing the extended system against the original without explanations. We do not compare against state-of-the-art baselines, and we omit ablation studies that isolate the explanation component's effect. Initial results suggest that users find the explanations understandable, but we observe no significant improvement in task completion or satisfaction. Due to the small sample and the absence of broader benchmarks, these findings are preliminary; future work would need a more extensive evaluation with multiple baselines and larger participant pools to draw stronger conclusions. Overall, the contribution is marginal, offering a modest, self-contained step toward explainable conversational recommenders.

title: Point-Voxel Set Attention for Context-Aware 3D Object Detection from Point Clouds
abstract: We present PVSA-RCNN, a 3D object detection framework that combines the strengths of point-based and voxel-based representations through a novel Point-Voxel Set Attention (PVSA) mechanism. Unlike previous methods that fuse voxel features to points via simple nearest-neighbor interpolation or repetitive convolutional blocks, PVSA explicitly models long-range dependencies and cross-scale interactions by computing set attention over a dynamic neighborhood of both raw points and voxel centers. This allows the detector to recover fine-grained geometric details lost in voxelization while also incorporating global contextual cues crucial for detecting occluded or distant objects. We further introduce a Context-Aware Proposal Refinement stage that re-weights proposal features using scene-level attention, effectively suppressing false positives. On the KITTI test set, our method achieves 81.4% mAP on car, 78.2% on pedestrian, and 75.9% on cyclist, outperforming PV-RCNN by 1.6%, 2.3%, and 1.8%, respectively. On the nuScenes test set, we obtain 68.5% mAP, exceeding the PV-RCNN baseline by 1.9 mAP points while maintaining a comparable inference speed of 82 ms per frame. Ablation studies confirm that each component contributes meaningfully. We note that performance degrades for extremely sparse points (e.g., greater than 50 m), which we plan to address by incorporating temporal fusion in future work.

title: Preliminary Experiments on Applying XLM-R to Cross-Lingual Document Classification in Tibetan
abstract: We present a preliminary exploration of applying the pre-trained multilingual encoder XLM-R to cross-lingual document classification for the Tibetan language, a low-resource language that has seen limited attention in prior work. Our approach directly uses the off-the-shelf XLM-R model to encode Tibetan documents and their English translations into a shared embedding space, and then performs nearest-neighbor classification in that space. We evaluate on a single, small dataset of 1,200 Tibetan news documents paired with English translations, which we collected from one online news source. Preliminary results show that the model achieves an accuracy of only 41.3%, which is barely above the majority-class baseline of 38.2% for our three-class problem. However, we did not compare against any other methods, nor did we perform fine-tuning or hyperparameter optimization. We also did not address the large domain shift between our dataset and the training data of XLM-R. These initial experiments highlight the need for more robust cross-lingual models for Tibetan, but we acknowledge that our findings are limited by the small dataset and the lack of comparative baselines. In future work, we plan to expand the dataset and include comparisons with multilingual BERT and other models.

title: FastPaD-RAG: Transferring a Privacy-Preserving Similarity Leakage Detection Protocol to Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: We present FastPaD-RAG, an incremental extension of the FastPaD protocol for detecting similarity-based leakage in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines. The original protocol was designed for password similarity checks in IoT services; here we adapt its core padded-similarity computation to dense text embeddings, replacing the password metric with cosine similarity over query and document vectors. A differential-privacy noise calibration is introduced to mask threshold violations during retrieval. The contribution is modest: we combine existing ideas from privacy-preserving similarity auditing and RAG reliability, without proposing a new problem or a fundamentally new method. We evaluate in a limited setting, using two small synthetic query sets derived from MS MARCO and TREC COVID, and compare only against a non-private baseline. We do not perform ablations on the noise calibration parameter, nor do we test against realistic attack models beyond a simple membership inference heuristic. Initial results suggest that leakage detection accuracy is comparable to the original FastPaD, but the privacy budget trade-off makes deployment impractical without further tuning. Overall, these findings are preliminary and would require substantial revision, including broader benchmarks and a rigorous comparison to existing leakage mitigation techniques, before the approach could be considered for practical use.

title: TempoGNN: Structural Pre-Training on Temporal Graphs for Early Fake News Detection
abstract: This paper introduces TempoGNN, a temporal graph neural network for early fake news detection that jointly exploits the structural and temporal dimensions of news propagation. Unlike existing propagation-based methods that rely on static graph snapshots, TempoGNN models dynamic user-news interactions through a continuous-time graph encoder. Its core contribution is a novel structural pre-training objective that learns transferable representations of propagation patterns from unlabeled temporal graphs via masked node and edge reconstruction, followed by task-specific fine-tuning on labeled fake news data. We evaluate TempoGNN on three public benchmarks, Twitter15, Twitter16, and Weibo, and compare it against several state-of-the-art baselines, including propagation-aware GCN and GAT models as well as existing fake news detectors. TempoGNN consistently achieves higher accuracy and F1 score, with the largest gains observed in early detection settings where only a few retweets are available. Ablation studies show that structural pre-training accelerates convergence and improves robustness to sparse user activity. A minor limitation is that the model relies on reliable timestamps for cascade construction, which may be noisy on certain platforms, yet the overall results indicate that TempoGNN provides a solid and practical solution for propagation-based fake news detection.

title: HandPrompt: Enhancing Video Action Recognition with Hand-Pose Guided Prompting in Image-Pretrained Transformers
abstract: We propose HandPrompt, a novel approach for video action recognition that adapts image-pretrained vision transformers using hand-pose cues. Unlike prior methods that require full fine-tuning or heavy temporal modules, we inject hand-keypoint prompts into the token sequence, enabling the model to capture fine-grained manipulative actions with minimal extra parameters. To exploit hand dynamics, we design a lightweight handmotion encoder that projects spatiotemporal hand-keypoint sequences into prompt tokens, which are then interleaved with frame patches. The resulting model retains the strong spatial priors of image models while gaining temporal sensitivity, and can be trained end-to-end on standard video datasets. We evaluate HandPrompt on Something-Something v2 and Epic-Kitchens 100, where it achieves top-1 accuracies of 68.3% and 43.7%, outperforming recent efficient video architectures such as AIM and Mformer, while requiring 3x fewer FLOPs. Ablations confirm that hand prompts contribute more than generic learned prompts on hand-oriented action classes. A limitation is that HandPrompt relies on a pre-trained hand detector, which may introduce errors in occluded scenes. Code and models will be released.

title: Leveraging Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Decoders for Low-Resource Machine Translation with Minimal Parallel Corpora
abstract: Recent work has shown that modest amounts of parallel data can yield usable machine translation systems when combined with careful curation. Meanwhile, hybrid Mamba-Transformer architectures have shown promise for efficient sequence modeling in large language models. We combine these two lines of work by adapting a hybrid Mamba-Transformer decoder to the minimal-data training recipe of prior work for low-resource machine translation. Specifically, we replace the standard Transformer decoder in a small NMT system with a Mamba-Transformer hybrid that interleaves selective state-space layers with attention layers, keeping the encoder and data pipeline unchanged. We evaluate on English-to-Nepali and English-to-Sinhala, using only 10K parallel sentences per pair and a shared subword vocabulary. Our experiments are limited to a single training seed and a 1,000-sentence test set, and we do not ablate the effect of data size or decoding hyperparameters. Initial results suggest a small but consistent BLEU improvement (0.8-1.2) for the hybrid decoder over a Transformer baseline on the Nepali pair, whereas on Sinhala the Mamba-only decoder performs best and the hybrid offers no gain. These findings are preliminary, and we do not claim superiority over strong back-translation baselines. Overall, the contribution is an incremental extension of minimal-data MT, and more extensive evaluation is needed.

title: Federated Averaging for Privacy-Preserving Vehicle Speed Prediction at the Edge: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a model without sharing raw data. In this paper, we apply a standard federated averaging (FedAvg) algorithm to a vehicular edge computing scenario for privacy-preserving vehicle speed prediction. We focus on a simple setup where roadside units act as clients and train a light-weight neural network on locally collected traffic data. We explore the feasibility of this straightforward application using a small public vehicle trajectory dataset, preprocessed into 90-second speed sequences from 50 vehicles across 3 days. Under a non-IID data split, we run initial experiments with FedAvg and report the resulting mean absolute error and convergence behavior. Our preliminary results show that federated training reaches a reasonable error level after about 100 communication rounds, though with noticeable variance across clients. We explicitly note that this is an initial exploration rather than a rigorous evaluation: we use a single small dataset, do not compare against centralized training or other federated algorithms, and do not address important practical issues such as client dropouts, heterogeneity in computation, or communication constraints. Future work will include larger benchmarks and stronger baselines.

title: DiscourseRotatE: Injecting Discourse Relations into RotatE for Multi-Hop Query Answering over Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Recent work on knowledge graph embeddings has shown that incorporating relational paths can improve multi-hop query answering. However, most path-based models treat all paths uniformly and ignore discourse cues present in natural language queries, such as concession, contrast, and temporal ordering. In this paper, we propose an incremental extension of the RotatE model, called DiscourseRotatE, that injects discourse relation embeddings derived from an off-the-shelf discourse parser into the composition function for multi-hop paths. The approach is a straightforward combination of existing techniques: discourse parsing features, relation path embeddings, and rotational distance scoring. We evaluate DiscourseRotatE in a limited setting using two benchmark subsets—WebQuestionsSP and a dialogue-based knowledge graph dataset—and compare against two standard baselines. We do not perform a full ablation, and attention-based and language model baselines are not included due to computational constraints. Initial results suggest that discourse-aware path weighting yields modest gains on queries containing explicit discourse connectives, but the improvements are inconsistent across relation types and dataset splits. Overall, the contribution is marginal and would require more extensive evaluation and a more principled integration of discourse structure to be competitive with state-of-the-art models.

title: Augmenting Instructional Videos for Procedural Activity Recognition via Distant Supervision and Learned Video Composition
abstract: Procedural activity recognition typically requires fine-grained annotations of step boundaries and labels, which are costly to obtain. Recent work leverages distant supervision from narrations in instructional videos to automatically generate pseudolabels for training, reducing annotation cost, while separate work has shown that learned video composition can provide effective data augmentation for action recognition. In this paper, we build on both lines of work and propose a method that combines distant supervision with a learned augmentation strategy for procedural activity recognition. Specifically, we adapt a video augmentation model originally designed for short action clips so that it can be applied to multi-step procedural videos, using the pseudolabels from a distantly supervised teacher model to guide the composition of training clips. We evaluate our approach on a subset of the Breakfast dataset, focusing on four activity categories, and report initial results. Our method shows modest gains over a strong baseline that uses the same distant supervision but no augmentation, suggesting that the two ideas are complementary. However, we do not outperform existing fully supervised state-of-the-art methods, and we lack an ablation of the individual components. In this limited setting, the results are promising yet inconclusive, and further study is required to assess generality.

title: Predicting Human Judgments of Instruction-Tuned Models from LLM-Estimated Data Utility: An Initial Study
abstract: Recent work has shown that language models can estimate the utility of pretraining data points for downstream performance, enabling efficient data mixture selection. In parallel, correlation studies find that standard NLP benchmarks align only weakly with human preferences. We extend the LLM-estimated utility approach, previously applied to pretraining, to the instruction-tuning setting and investigate whether aggregate utility scores predict human evaluations of tuned model variants. Using a single base model and a small set of candidate instruction-tuning mixtures, we compute utility scores for each mixture, lightly tune variants on those mixtures, and compare the resulting utility-based ranking against human ratings on a limited set of 50 prompts. We observe a moderate positive correlation in one of three configurations, while the remaining configurations show no significant relationship. Our evaluation is restricted to one base model, a single utility estimator, and no hyperparameter ablations or baseline comparisons. These initial results suggest that LLM-estimated utility may carry signal about human-perceived quality, but the effect is unreliable and potentially confounded by model capacity. Moreover, the utility estimator was not designed for instruction-following data, which may limit transfer. Overall, this work is a modest first step toward connecting data-centric optimization to human evaluation, but it requires substantial revision and broader validation to establish dependable predictions.

title: Budget-Aware Tool-Use with Stability-Inducing Weight Perturbation for Multi-LLM Agent Teams
abstract: We propose a modest extension to budget-aware tool-use that couples it with stability-inducing weight perturbation (STAR) for multi-LLM agent teams. Our method, STAR-Tool, applies a regularization penalty derived from the Fisher information of the tool-selection policy to reduce catastrophic forgetting when agents are adapted to new tasks under a shared token budget. Unlike prior work that treats tool-use budgeting as a single-agent optimization problem, we use a simple cooperative scheduling rule and adjust the perturbation magnitude per agent. We evaluate STAR-Tool on two subsets of a tool-augmented reasoning benchmark in a limited setting: three LLM agents and a fixed budget. Initial results suggest that STAR-Tool can preserve tool selection accuracy on seen tasks slightly better than a budget-aware baseline and an unregularized multi-agent variant, while keeping average task completion cost comparable. However, the gains are consistent only for the smaller agent configuration and do not translate to the larger model suite; we also did not run full ablations on the perturbation schedule. Because our evaluation is limited and the contribution is primarily a combination of existing components, these results should be viewed as preliminary. We discuss several limitations and potential revisions.

title: Counterfactual Knowledge Editing for Temporal Legal Fact Updates in a Small QA Model: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Recent work in knowledge editing has shown that counterfactual factual updates can be injected into language models through direct weight modification. In this paper, we apply a standard counterfactual knowledge editing method—specifically the rank-one model editing approach—to a small legal question-answering model, with the goal of updating outdated statutory references and case citations. Our motivation is to explore whether this widely used editing technique transfers to a narrowly scoped domain where facts change over time. We collect a single small dataset of 300 temporal legal fact pairs from an online legal database and perform initial experiments. We do not compare against any baseline editing methods, fine-tuning, or retrieval-based approaches. We find that a substantial fraction of edits fail to generalize to paraphrased queries, and that editing one fact sometimes degrades performance on unrelated nearby facts. These preliminary results suggest that straightforward application of the method yields limited reliability in this setting. We conclude by noting the need for more careful evaluation and domain-specific adaptation, and we explicitly refrain from making strong claims about the usefulness of the approach.

title: PolyMatch: Semi-Supervised Referring Image Segmentation via Polygon-Sequence Consistency
abstract: Recent referring image segmentation methods predict masks by generating polygon vertex sequences, which avoids pixel-wise decoding and improves boundary quality. However, these methods rely on large amounts of expensive mask annotations. We present PolyMatch, a semi-supervised framework that adapts a polygon-sequence decoder for referring segmentation to settings with only a fraction of the RefCOCO-type annotations labeled. PolyMatch is built on a student-teacher architecture with a shared vision-language encoder. The teacher produces pseudo polygon sequences for unlabeled images under weak augmentation, and the student is supervised to match these sequences under strong augmentation. To prevent drift in the polygon coordinate space, we combine a point-wise L1 loss with a directed Chamfer distance between sampled polygon edges, and we further regularize the intermediate visual features with a contrastive loss between matched referring expressions and image regions. We evaluate PolyMatch on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg using 1%, 5%, and 10% labeled training samples. PolyMatch consistently outperforms fully supervised training on the labeled subset and strong semi-supervised baselines including FixMatch and UniMatch, improving mIoU by up to 5.3 points with 5% labels. We also show that the polygon-based consistency loss yields larger gains than mask-based consistency. One limitation is the extra decoding cost of polygon generation, which we mitigate by early stopping the vertex decoder during inference.

title: Extending TextSeal to Multilingual ASR Transcripts: A Preliminary Study of Error-Induced Watermark Degradation
abstract: Recent advances in multilingual speech recognition have made it possible to transcribe hundreds of languages, raising concerns about unauthorized use of transcripts in training large language models. Existing text watermarking methods like TextSeal embed provenance signals in generated text, but their behavior under automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors is not well understood. We propose a simple extension that applies TextSeal's entropy-based token selection to multilingual ASR transcripts, accounting for the confidence scores of a multilingual ASR model such as Omnilingual ASR. We evaluate the method on five languages from the Common Voice dataset and a synthetic noise condition. Our initial results suggest that watermark detection accuracy degrades significantly in the presence of ASR errors, particularly for low-resource languages with higher character error rates. We also observe that the localized watermarking property of TextSeal is partially retained in clean conditions. The study is limited in scope: we only test a fixed bit budget and a single ASR model, and we do not compare against adversarial attacks or paraphrase robustness. Overall, the findings are preliminary but indicate that naively adapting text watermarks to ASR outputs is not sufficient, and further work is needed to design error-resilient watermarking schemes for speech-to-text pipelines.

title: A3C-DPG: Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic with Delayed Policy Updates for Continuous Control
abstract: Asynchronous advantage actor-critic (A3C) has proven an effective and lightweight paradigm for parallel deep reinforcement learning, yet its on-policy nature limits its sample efficiency in continuous control. Off-policy deterministic policy gradient methods such as DDPG achieve state-of-the-art performance in many continuous tasks, but they are usually trained in a synchronous, single-agent fashion. In this paper, we propose A3C-DPG, an incremental combination of these two families. The algorithm maintains a set of asynchronous actor workers that collect transitions and write them to a shared replay buffer, while a single learner applies deterministic policy gradient updates with a pair of slowly moving target networks. To mitigate the overestimation bias inherent in deterministic value functions, we delay the policy update relative to the critic update, following recent suggestions. We evaluate A3C-DPG on two standard benchmark tasks (HalfCheetah-v2 and Hopper-v2) with a fixed number of 16 workers. In our limited experiments, the proposed method reaches a return comparable to single-threaded DDPG but did not consistently beat a well-tuned TD3 baseline. There is also no clear evidence that asynchronous collection yields a wall-clock speedup over a single learner in our setup. We have not performed ablations of the replay buffer size or the update delay, and our results cover only two environments. These initial findings are thus preliminary and suggest that further engineering and hyperparameter tuning would be needed to make asynchronous off-policy updates practical.

title: Value-Guided Decoding with Modular Transformers: A Preliminary Study on Efficiency and Preference Trade-offs
abstract: Recent work has shown that value-guided Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) decoding can improve the preference alignment of generated text, while modular transformers offer a flexible way to compress large models for efficient inference by routing inputs through a subset of layers. In this paper, we combine these two ideas, using a modular transformer as the policy model within a value-guided MCTS decoding framework, with the goal of reducing inference cost while maintaining gains in text preference. We conduct an initial evaluation on a single summarization dataset and one base model, comparing against standard beam search and value-guided decoding with a dense transformer. Our results are mixed: the modular value-guided approach achieves modest improvements in preference metrics over beam search, but the expected speed-ups are only partially realized due to the overhead of MCTS rollouts. We do not yet provide ablations on different modularization granularities or value model sizes, and the study is limited to a single domain. These initial results suggest that the combination has potential, but substantial further investigation is needed to determine when and how modular value-guided decoding can be practically beneficial.

title: Pre-Training Plain Vision Transformers for Detection via Masked Patch Substitution
abstract: We present Masked Patch Substitution (MPS), a self-supervised pre-training method for plain Vision Transformer backbones in object detection and instance segmentation. MPS randomly replaces a subset of input patches with learned prototype embeddings and tasks the network with predicting the original features, encouraging both low-level reconstruction and high-level semantic grouping. Unlike MAE, which discards masked patches, MPS retains the full token sequence, avoiding the pre-training/fine-tuning gap and enabling seamless use with structured detectors such as Mask R-CNN and ViTDet. On COCO and LVIS, we show that plain ViT-B and ViT-L backbones pre-trained with MPS improve detection and segmentation AP by up to +1.5 over MAE pre-training and +0.8 over ImageNet-1k supervised pre-training, with larger gains for the ViT-L backbone. A scaling study demonstrates that MPS benefits from increased pre-training compute and data, reaching 58.2 box AP on COCO with ViT-L and a 2B token corpus. We also analyze the effect of prototype granularity and replacement ratio. A minor limitation is that MPS has only been evaluated on detection and segmentation; its transfer to other dense prediction tasks remains unexplored. Our code and models will be released.

title: Applying Structured Chain-of-Thought Prompting to R Script Generation for Statistical Analysis: A Preliminary Study
abstract: In this paper, we apply Structured Chain-of-Thought prompting, an established technique for code generation, to a new domain: generating R scripts for statistical analysis from natural language descriptions. We collect a small dataset of 120 problem statements from introductory statistics courses and evaluate the approach using GPT-4. Without modifying the prompting methodology, we explore how well this method transfers to this domain. Preliminary results show that the method achieves a pass@1 of 34.2%, indicating moderate capability. However, this is an initial exploration with several limitations: our dataset is small and not representative of real-world statistical coding tasks; we do not compare against any baseline methods or alternative prompting strategies; and the evaluation is conducted with a single model and a single run. Furthermore, we do not analyze failure cases or the effect of different prompt formulations. These limitations preclude any strong claims. Nonetheless, we believe this work provides insights for future research on applying general-purpose code generation methods to specialized domains. We release our dataset and evaluation scripts for reproducibility.

title: EditNet: Multi-Scale Time Series Forecasting of Developer Edits in AI-Assisted Programming
abstract: AI code assistants are increasingly ubiquitous, yet their impact on developer productivity is hard to measure because edit behavior is bursty and highly non-stationary. In this work, we tackle the forecasting of developer edit streams as a multi-scale time series problem, and introduce EditNet, a transformer-based architecture that captures both short-term burstiness and long-term drift in code modification activity. EditNet uses a temporal convolutional stem to extract local features, followed by a self-attention module over the most recent edit sessions.
