We train and evaluate EditNet on two large-scale benchmarks: RealEdit-53.6K, a corpus of 53.6K real-world edits made by developers to AI-generated code, and CommitStream, a public dataset of commit events. EditNet achieves 18.4% lower mean absolute error (MAE) than the best baseline (Toto 2.0 zero-shot) on RealEdit-53.6K and 23.7% lower MAE on CommitStream, while being 3.2x more parameter-efficient than the leading foundation model. We also show that EditNet's attention weights align with known patterns of post-acceptance refactoring. Limitations include a focus on per-session counts rather than individual keystrokes, and the fact that both benchmarks mainly reflect developer activity in production environments. We release our code and pre-trained checkpoints.

title: A Streaming Algorithm for Maximum Estimation with Heavy-Hitter Pre-Filtering in Sliding Windows
abstract: We study the problem of estimating the maximum value in a sliding window over a high-velocity data stream. While classical streaming algorithms maintain exact or approximate maxima, they require per-element processing that is costly when the window is large. We propose an incremental combination of heavy-hitter detection and max tracking, where a Misra-Gries-style counter is used to prune non-candidates before the max operation. This extends the deterministic heavy-hitters literature to the maximum-estimation setting. We evaluate the method on synthetic Zipfian and uniform streams in a limited setting, comparing against a naive max-retaining baseline and an exact window scan. Initial results suggest that our method reduces per-element update time by up to 40% while maintaining bounded overestimation errors on skewed data. However, the trade-off is sensitive to the window length and the choice of the heavy-hitter threshold, and we do not yet provide a theoretical regret bound. The evaluation is also restricted to a single synthetic workload; we have not tested on real-world traces, nor have we implemented a comparison against sketching-based alternatives. These limitations indicate that substantial revision is needed before the approach can be considered for production deployment.

title: Applying AIM to Hand Gesture Recognition: A Preliminary Study on a Small Custom Dataset
abstract: In this work, we apply AIM, a recently proposed method for adapting image models to video action recognition, to the domain of hand gesture recognition. AIM was originally developed and evaluated on large-scale action recognition benchmarks, and here we explore whether it can transfer to a visually focused task involving only hands. We collect a small custom dataset of 500 video clips covering 10 gesture classes, including common signs and fine-grained finger movements. We train AIM using a frozen image backbone and a lightweight temporal adapter, and our initial experiments achieve a top-1 accuracy of 62.3%. However, we do not compare against any existing hand gesture recognition methods, and we observe several limitations: the model often confuses visually similar gestures, is sensitive to background clutter, and degrades significantly when hands are partially occluded. These are preliminary results, and we explicitly acknowledge that the small dataset size and lack of baseline comparisons limit the generalizability of our findings. The contribution is a straightforward application of an existing method to a new domain, with no methodological novelty, and we view this as an initial exploration rather than a definitive study.

title: LC-Align: Language-Conditioned Canonical Alignment for Massively Multilingual Sentence Embeddings
abstract: Massively multilingual sentence embeddings such as SONAR and NLLB encode thousands of languages into a shared space, yet retrieval and classification quality drops sharply for low-resource languages. We propose LC-Align, a language-conditioned canonical alignment method that learns a lightweight orthogonal transformation per language to map pretrained embeddings into a common canonical space. Unlike prior contrastive approaches that require large parallel corpora, LC-Align is trained on a small set of high-resource pivot languages using a bi-directional cycle-consistency objective, and it can be applied zero-shot to languages unseen during alignment training. We evaluate on multilingual sentence retrieval (Tatoeba, BUCC), zero-shot XNLI, and a new 300-language semantic similarity test set built from translated parallel sentences. LC-Align improves average recall@1 by 8.4 points over SONAR and 12.1 points over LaBSE on low-resource languages, while retaining within-language performance. On XNLI, LC-Align yields a 3.9 point absolute accuracy improvement for the lowest-resource language families. We further show that the learned transformations are complementary to existing embedding alignment, giving gains in a downstream NMT reranking task. Limitations include reliance on a small parallel evaluation set and remaining degradation for languages outside the training distribution. Our code, model, and evaluation data are public.

title: Graph Isomorphism-Based Architecture Augmentation for Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search in Facial Expression Recognition
abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) has shown promise for automated design of deep models for facial expression recognition (FER). Recent work introduced graph isomorphism-based architecture augmentation to enhance performance predictors in NAS, improving ranking accuracy with limited computational cost. In this paper, we combine these two directions by applying architecture augmentation to an evolutionary NAS framework for FER. Specifically, we augment the predictor training set with isomorphic variants of evaluated architectures, intending to regularize the predictor and mitigate overfitting when the search space is small. We evaluate our approach on FER2013, a widely used benchmark, with a restricted search space of only 1,024 architectures. Initial results suggest a modest improvement in predictor ranking accuracy and final accuracy of the discovered architecture compared to training without augmentation. However, our evaluation is limited: we use only one dataset, a single search space, and do not compare against standard NAS baselines or ablate the augmentation ratio. Moreover, graph isomorphism augmentation may introduce redundant training samples, and its effectiveness under larger search spaces remains unclear. Overall, this is a preliminary study indicating that architecture augmentation can be beneficial for FER NAS, but substantial further validation and ablations are required to confirm the findings.

title: Safety-Aware Decoding for Vision-Language Models: A Preliminary Study on Multimodal Jailbreak Resistance
abstract: As vision-language models (VLMs) become widely deployed, their vulnerability to multimodal jailbreak attacks—where adversarial images are crafted to bypass safety alignment—poses a serious risk. While safety-aware decoding methods like SafeDecoding have proven effective for text-only LLMs, their adaptation to the multimodal setting remains underexplored. In this paper, we extend SafeDecoding to VLMs by introducing a safety expert model that conditions on both visual and textual embeddings to adjust the next-token distribution during generation. We evaluate our method on a restricted set of four jailbreak attack types drawn from a publicly available multimodal safety benchmark, using LLaVA-1.5 and MiniGPT-4 as base models. Our results show an average reduction in attack success rate of 14.7% across the tested attacks, but with considerable variance: the method performs well on text-only attacks and image-text mismatch attacks, yet offers negligible improvement on adversarially perturbed images. We also conduct a small human preference study (N=20) comparing safety-aware and baseline outputs; participants show a slight preference for the former, though the difference does not reach statistical significance. We do not perform ablations on the safety expert's training data size or architecture, and we suspect the expert may not generalize to unseen attack vectors. These initial results suggest that transferring safety-aware decoding to multimodal inputs is feasible, but substantially more robust evaluation and refinement are needed before practical deployment.

title: Temporal Equivalence Reward Modeling for 3D Human Pose Estimation
abstract: We introduce Temporal Equivalence Reward Modeling (TERM), a new learning paradigm for 3D human pose estimation that directly optimizes temporal coherence and anatomical plausibility. Unlike prior methods that rely on hand-crafted pose priors or adversarial losses, TERM formulates the problem of learning a reward model over pose sequences. This reward model, trained on million-scale synthetic motion capture data, learns a semantic equivalence function that identities nonlinearly warped poses representing the same underlying motion. We use TERM as (i) a re-ranking target to select the most consistent pose sequence from candidate outputs of any backbone estimator, and (ii) a dense auxiliary reward for policy-gradient fine-tuning. TERM introduces a novel problem: reward modeling for spatio-temporal pose dynamics, with a new evaluation protocol. On Human3.6M, TERM reduces MPJPE from 50.2mm to 48.1mm over the strong baseline TCPFormer; on MPI-INF-3DHP, it raises the AUC from 84.1% to 87.6%; and on 3DPW, it improves MPJPE from 72.9mm to 68.3mm. TERM also generalizes across backbones, improving VideoPose3D by 3.1mm and PoseMAE by 2.4mm on Human3.6M. Our code and models are publicly available.

title: Applying Token-Level Policy Optimization to Code-Mixed Speech-to-Text Dialogue Models: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We apply token-level policy optimization (TLPO), originally proposed for mitigating language confusion in large language models, to the setting of end-to-end speech-to-text dialogue models operating on code-mixed speech. Our motivation is that code-mixed speech exhibits frequent language switches that may induce the same confusion patterns observed in text-based LLMs. We adapt the existing TLPO objective directly to the spoken model's decoder, with no changes to the method itself. Initial experiments are conducted on a single small dataset of 500 code-mixed Hindi-English spoken dialogues, collected from publicly available sources. We evaluate only the adapted model's word error rate and language-confusion rate, without comparison to any baselines. Preliminary results suggest that TLPO can reduce language confusion in some utterance types, but the improvements are inconsistent across samples. Limitations include the small dataset size, lack of baselines, and the fact that we did not tune hyperparameters for the speech setting. Overall, this work is a straightforward application of an existing method to a new domain, and further investigation is needed to draw robust conclusions.

title: LEAP: Language-Embedded Adaptation for Policy Transfer across Visual and Dynamics Domains
abstract: We introduce LEAP, a method that leverages large-scale language models to construct a shared task-embedding space, enabling a policy to be primed with relevant experiences from a library of prior tasks. By treating language as a task interface, LEAP identifies and recombines sub-skills from heterogeneous demonstration data, facilitating sample-efficient adaptation to new environments and dynamics. Our experiments on three benchmarks—Meta-World, the Franka kitchen domain, and a high-speed driving simulator—demonstrate that LEAP significantly outperforms strong baselines, including goal-conditioned RL, prior transfer methods, and model-agnostic meta-learning, achieving up to a 60% reduction in interactions needed to reach a target performance level. We further analyze robustness to language annotation noise and visual distribution shift, showing that LEAP retains superior performance under these perturbations. The main limitations of our approach are its reliance on a pre-trained language encoder and the requirement for a small set of target-domain demonstrations. Overall, LEAP provides a practical and scalable framework for language-conditioned policy transfer, with clear benefits in sample efficiency and robustness across diverse autonomous control tasks.

title: EERL: Event-Enhanced Reinforcement Learning for Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning with LLM-Generated Semantic Tags
abstract: We propose EERL, a novel framework that integrates large language model (LLM)-based event extraction with reinforcement learning to improve multi-hop reasoning over temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs). TKG reasoning requires capturing both structural and temporal contexts, but existing RL methods rely on static embeddings or overlook event semantics. EERL first uses an LLM to extract event-centric semantic tags from text sources, which are aligned with TKG entities and relations via a contrastive learning module. These tags are then injected as auxiliary edge features into a temporal graph neural network, and an adaptive policy network is trained with inductive embeddings to select effective reasoning paths. We evaluate EERL on three benchmarks (ICEWS14, ICEWS18, and GDELT) for the time-aware link prediction task. EERL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including ARLIE, TANGO, and DSTAG, achieving up to 8.3% relative improvement in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and 6.1% in Hits@1, while maintaining comparable training efficiency. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component. We also discuss limitations, including the dependency on text coverage and the computational overhead of LLM inference, which we mitigate via caching. The results demonstrate that integrating event semantics with RL-based reasoning yields robust and interpretable temporal predictions.

title: A Preliminary Study on Transferring Vision-Language Models for Fine-Grained Action Recognition in Procedural Videos
abstract: We explore the use of pre-trained vision-language models for fine-grained action recognition in procedural videos. While recent work has shown strong performance on generic action recognition, their application to domain-specific procedural activities remains under-explored. We propose a simple yet effective method that adapts a vision-language model by generating pseudo-labels from video-language alignment and then fine-tuning on target procedures. This leverages distant supervision without manual annotations. Our approach extends existing work by incorporating a lightweight temporal aggregation module. We evaluate on a single benchmark, the CrossTask dataset, and compare against a limited set of baselines. Initial results suggest moderate improvements over the base model, but we observe instability across different backbone initializations and temporal aggregation choices. We do not perform full ablation studies or evaluate on multiple datasets due to computational constraints. The findings are preliminary and require further investigation to confirm generalizability. Overall, this study highlights the potential of vision-language transfer for procedural activity recognition, but substantial refinement is needed to achieve robust performance.

title: Combining Lexical Data Augmentation with Reinforced Self-Training for Low-Resource Multilingual Machine Translation
abstract: Multilingual machine translation models often underperform on low-resource language pairs, and recent work has shown that lexical data augmentation (e.g., Bilex Rx) and reinforced self-training (ReST) can each yield gains in different settings. In this paper, we propose a simple extension that combines both ideas: an alternating training procedure where the target side of synthetic translation data is rephrased using a bilingual lexicon, and the model is updated via a REINFORCE-style objective with rewards computed against a small development reference set. This is an incremental combination of existing components rather than a new method. We evaluate in a limited setting on four low-resource language pairs from FLORES-200 using a 300M-parameter multilingual encoder-decoder. Compared to a standard pretrained baseline, the combined approach improves average ChrF by 0.6, and it slightly outperforms either component applied alone. However, we do not compare against strong recent systems such as NLLB, and we do not ablate important design choices including reward scaling, lexicon thresholding, or sampling temperature. Initial results suggest that the gains are modest and concentrated on languages with larger available lexicons. We believe this direction is promising, but the current evidence is inconclusive and would require substantially more evaluation across languages, model sizes, and baselines.

title: Combining Self-Supervised Pre-training and Implicit Neural Representations for Few-Shot Time-Series Classification
abstract: Self-supervised pre-training has shown promise for few-shot classification in audio and image domains. In this paper, we extend this approach to time-series classification by combining a large-scale self-supervised pre-training objective with a meta-learned encoder based on implicit neural representations. Our method, which we call INR-FSL, encodes each time-series instance as a continuous function and learns to adapt to new classes via a prototypical network. We evaluate on three publicly available time-series datasets (ECG200, Wafer, and FordA) and compare against a standard fine-tuning baseline and a feature-wise pre-training baseline. In our limited experiments, INR-FSL achieves modest gains in accuracy on two of the three datasets, with an average improvement of 2.1 percentage points over fine-tuning. However, the gains are inconsistent across domains, and we observe that the implicit representation adds significant computational overhead. We do not include ablations on the pre-training objective or meta-learning schedule, and we do not compare to more recent transformer-based methods. Our initial results suggest that implicit neural representations can complement self-supervised pre-training for few-shot time-series classification, but substantial further investigation is needed to understand when and why this combination helps.

title: Value-Guided Evidence Aggregation: Monte-Carlo Tree Search for Long-Document Retrieval
abstract: Long-document retrieval often loses critical evidence when a single document must be split into chunks: a single vector representation cannot capture all relevant passages, and existing chunk aggregation methods rely on heuristics or task-specific supervision that do not account for downstream answer quality. We propose Value-Guided Monte-Carlo Evidence Aggregation (VG-MCEA), a method that frames chunk selection as a sequential decision process and uses a learned value model to guide Monte-Carlo Tree Search over candidate chunk combinations. VG-MCEA iteratively expands and evaluates evidence sets, directly optimizing for the expected answer relevance of the retrieved package rather than independent chunk scores. We train the value model on a small set of annotated (query, document, answer) triples and apply it without fine-tuning the underlying retriever or generator. On three long-document QA benchmarks — HotpotQA, Natural Questions long-document split, and TREC-CAR — VG-MCEA improves answer F1 by 3.1–4.7 points over state-of-the-art chunk aggregation baselines and increases recall at 64 tokens by up to 6.2 points, while requiring only 15% of the inference time of exhaustive reranking. Ablations confirm that the value signal and tree search each contribute meaningfully. Limitations include sensitivity to chunk granularity and additional decoding overhead, but the method offers a general, scoring-model-agnostic strategy for evidence aggregation.

title: Applying DDS2M Self-Supervised Denoising Diffusion to Hyperspectral Video Restoration: Initial Experiments on a Small Dataset
abstract: We present a straightforward application of the DDS2M self-supervised denoising diffusion spatio-spectral model, originally designed for hyperspectral image restoration, to the task of hyperspectral video restoration. We directly leverage the existing framework without any methodological modifications or novel components. Our initial experiments are conducted on a single small dataset consisting of 30 hyperspectral video sequences with synthetic noise. We evaluate the restoration quality using PSNR and SSIM, but do not include comparisons with any baseline methods. The goal of this work is to explore whether the spatio-spectral diffusion prior from DDS2M can transfer to the temporal setting of video data. Our preliminary results indicate that the model produces visually acceptable restorations, but quantitatively the performance degrades for frames with large motion, and the lack of temporal modeling leads to flickering artifacts. We explicitly acknowledge that the single small dataset and the absence of baseline comparisons limit the interpretability and generalizability of these findings. This study serves as an initial exploration and does not claim state-of-the-art performance. We hope to address these limitations in future work by incorporating temporal modules and evaluating on larger benchmarks.

title: Applying a Contrastive Gender-Debiasing Method to English–Kurmanji Machine Translation: A Preliminary Study on a Small Test Set
abstract: In this paper, we apply a target-agnostic gender-aware contrastive learning approach, originally designed for multilingual machine translation, directly to English-to-Kurmanji translation, a low-resource language pair, without any methodological changes. We explore whether this existing method can mitigate gender bias in translation output when training data is scarce. Our initial experiments use a single small test set consisting of 200 sentence pairs with ambiguous gender references, and we fine-tune a pre-trained multilingual model using the contrastive objective. We then evaluate translations for gender accuracy and fluency. However, this work is preliminary and has clear limitations: we do not include any baseline comparisons, and the dataset is too small to support robust conclusions. Furthermore, the contrastive examples used for fine-tuning are limited in diversity, and our evaluation is based on a small set of sentences, which may not represent the broader challenges of Kurmanji. Results are mixed; we observe minor improvements for some pronoun categories but no consistent overall gain. We therefore view our findings as exploratory and caution against generalization. We release our data and code, but we stress that the effectiveness of the method in low-resource domains remains an open question. Future work with larger datasets and baseline methods is necessary.

title: Asynchronous Bayesian Optimization for Automated Hyperparameter Tuning of Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents
abstract: We introduce AsyncBO-RL, a Bayesian optimization framework for automated hyperparameter tuning of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents. Unlike traditional Bayesian optimization, which evaluates hyperparameter configurations synchronously, AsyncBO-RL supports asynchronous evaluations in a distributed setting, making it well suited for computationally expensive RL training runs. A key innovation is a censored surrogate model that ingests partially completed training runs, improving data efficiency without requiring full rollouts. We pair this model with a resource-aware acquisition function that balances exploration, exploitation, and early stopping. On three continuous control benchmarks (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d), we tune the hyperparameters of PPO and DDPG. AsyncBO-RL consistently outperforms random search and standard Bayesian optimization in terms of wall-clock time and final return, and matches or exceeds hand-tuned baselines across all test environments. We also demonstrate robustness to evaluation noise. A limitation is that our experiments are limited to simulated control tasks; applying the method to real-world systems is an area for future work. Overall, AsyncBO-RL provides a practical, sample-efficient solution for RL hyperparameter tuning.

title: Applying DSTAG to Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion for Historical Maritime Trade: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We apply DSTAG, a semantic tag-enhanced dual-graph convolutional network originally designed for temporal knowledge graph completion, to a newly assembled temporal knowledge graph of historical maritime trade routes. This dataset is small, containing 1,200 entities and 8,000 timestamped facts across 20 years. Our goal is to evaluate the direct transferability of the model to a new domain without any methodological adaptation. Preliminary results show that the model achieves a mean reciprocal rank of 0.23, which is lower than the performance reported on the original benchmark. We do not include baseline comparisons because no established temporal knowledge graph completion baselines have yet been applied to this domain, and the dataset's small scale limits the reliability of any comparative evaluation. We also identify several limitations: the semantic tags required by DSTAG must be manually constructed for this domain, the temporal granularity of shipping records is irregular, and the model's attention mechanism does not capture the periodicity of trade cycles. Our initial experiments suggest that direct application of an existing model to a niche domain without domain-specific adjustments yields suboptimal results. This work is an exploratory application rather than a methodological contribution; we intend it to serve as a starting point for future adaptation efforts.

title: Language-Guided Pseudo-Label Denoising for Semantic Segmentation in Adverse Driving Conditions
abstract: Self-training with pseudo-labels is a prominent approach to semantic segmentation for autonomous driving, but its accuracy degrades rapidly when pseudo-labels are corrupted under adverse weather and lighting. We propose LGSeg, a vision-language guided denoising framework that enhances self-training robustness by leveraging pre-trained vision-language models to identify and correct noisy pseudo-labels. For each training image, we extract class-aligned text embeddings and compute patch-wise alignment scores between image features and each class description. These scores act as a reliability prior for the predicted mask, and we introduce a dynamic masking mechanism that adaptively excludes or rectifies low-confidence regions before they are used as supervision. To further reduce error accumulation, we perturb the alignment distribution with a lightweight denoising network that refines unreliable predictions in both feature and label space. We evaluate LGSeg on Cityscapes and the Adverse Conditions Dataset (ACDC) for fog, night, and rain scenarios. Our method improves mean IoU by 3.2% and 4.1% over a strong self-training baseline and outperforms recent pseudo-label denoising approaches across all conditions. A key limitation is the added computational cost of online VLM inference, which we mitigate with a distilled student. We will release code and models.

title: Conformal Tool Selection for LLM Agents under Imperfect Instructions: A Case Study on Web Navigation
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on tool-use policies to complete complex tasks; however, their performance degrades when user-provided instructions are ambiguous or partially incorrect. In this work, we extend conformal prediction—an established framework for distribution-free uncertainty quantification—to the task of tool selection in LLM agents. We propose a lightweight calibration step that adjusts the agent's confidence scores over candidate tools, producing a selectable set of tools that is guaranteed to contain the correct tool with high marginal probability. On a single web-navigation benchmark with synthetically corrupted instructions, we show that conformalized tool selection reduces failure rate by a modest margin compared to a greedy baseline. We do not include additional benchmarks, ablations, or comparisons with alternative uncertainty methods; the evaluation is restricted to one domain and one agent backbone. Initial results suggest that the approach is promising, but the improvement is within the noise of our limited setup, and substantial refinement—including better calibration objectives, broader evaluation, and integration with downstream planning—would be needed to draw firm conclusions. Overall, this work constitutes an incremental step toward reliable tool use in LLM agents under imperfect guidance.

title: Function-Space Bayesian Continual Learning with Pre-Trained Feature Priming
abstract: We propose a novel method for continual learning that combines function-space variational inference with pre-trained feature abstractions. Our approach, called Bayesian Primed Function-Space (BPFS), maintains a distribution over functions rather than parameters, enabling principled uncertainty estimation and mitigating catastrophic forgetting. We introduce a feature-priming mechanism that transfers representations from a pre-trained backbone to the function-space prior, allowing the model to rapidly adapt to new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. We evaluate BPFS on standard continual learning benchmarks, including Split CIFAR-100, Split Tiny ImageNet, and a continual domain-incremental scenario. Compared to established baselines such as Elastic Weight Consolidation, Variational Continual Learning, and Functional Regularization of Continual Learning, BPFS achieves consistently higher average accuracy and lower forgetting. Our ablation studies show the contribution of each component. We also demonstrate that BPFS is robust to varying pre-training qualities and task orders. A limitation is the increased computational cost due to function-space inference, although this is acceptable for moderate model sizes. Overall, BPFS provides a solid step toward scalable Bayesian continual learning with strong empirical performance.

title: Self-Corrective Conversational Recommender Agents via Learned World Models of User Preference Dynamics
abstract: Conversational recommender systems (CRS) must balance eliciting user preferences and making accurate suggestions under uncertainty. While recent methods use large language models for dialogue generation, they lack explicit modeling of how user preferences evolve as the conversation progresses. We propose WM-CRS, a conversational recommendation agent that learns a lightweight world model of user preference dynamics from dialogue context and historical interaction data. The world model enables (1) counterfactual rollouts to evaluate candidate items before asking, and (2) a test-time self-correction mechanism that refines the agent's policy when predicted outcomes diverge from observed user feedback. We integrate WM-CRS with both template-based and LLM-based response generators, requiring no additional annotation. On the ReDial and GoRecDial benchmarks, WM-CRS improves recommendation hit@10 by 8.2% and 11.4% relative over strong baselines (BARCOR, CRM, and KBRD), while increasing dialogue success rate by 6.3 percentage points on average. Ablations confirm that the world model's counterfactual rollouts contribute most to gains in cold-start scenarios. Limitations include evaluation on only two benchmarks and reliance on synthetic user feedback for self-correction; future work will extend to live user studies and multi-domain catalogs.

title: SparseInstrucNav: Instruction-Aware Fuzzy Pruning for Efficient Egocentric Visual Navigation
abstract: Egocentric visual navigation agents often rely on dense frame-by-frame reasoning, which is computationally expensive and exposes the model to irrelevant distractors. We present SparseInstrucNav, a method that dynamically prunes both spatial and channel dimensions of video frames using a fuzzy sparsity formulation, conditioned on natural-language navigation instructions. Our framework employs a lightweight instruction-following gate, built on a multimodal large language model, to estimate the relevance of each input frame to the current navigation subgoal. Frames with low relevance are aggressively pruned, while informative regions are retained via fuzzy channel selection. We integrate SparseInstrucNav into a transformer-based navigation policy and train it end-to-end with a sparse-aware loss. On the R2R benchmark and the indoor-instruction subset of Ego4D, SparseInstrucNav outperforms prior navigation policies (e.g., DUET and VLN-BERT) by 4.1% and 3.3% in success rate, respectively, while cutting FLOPs by 32% and improving inference speed by 1.8x. We also show that our pruning strategy transfers across environments, though we observe a small accuracy drop when the instruction distribution shifts to highly ambiguous wording. Our work demonstrates that instruction-aware fuzzy frame pruning is a practical and effective approach for real-time egocentric navigation.

title: Term-Aware Curriculum Selection for Low-Resource Clinical Machine Translation with Fairness Evaluation
abstract: We present a targeted fine-tuning framework for machine translation (MT) in the clinical domain, specifically designed for low-resource conditions. Our method, called term-aware curriculum selection (TACS), leverages a small set of in-domain sentences prioritized by medical term frequency and lexical diversity, combined with a lightweight adapter module that is inserted into a frozen pretrained MT model. We evaluate TACS on two clinical translation benchmarks: a new dermatology-focused English-to-French/Portuguese test set extracted from patient education materials, and the public UF Medical Clinical Translation corpus. In experiments with as few as 1,000 training sentences, TACS improves BLEU by an average of 4.2 points over a strong unsupervised baseline (M2M-100) and outperforms full fine-tuning of the same model with 10x more data, reducing training cost by 80%. We also perform a fairness analysis across patient demographic subgroups using a novel composite metric, showing that TACS yields more consistent error rates than baselines. Limitations include a narrow language pair coverage and reliance on automatically extracted terminology. Our results demonstrate that with a principled data selection strategy, practical clinical MT is achievable using minimal human-annotated data.

title: Retrieval-Guided Weight Interpolation for Continual Learning under Covariate Shift
abstract: Recent work in continual learning has explored both adapter routing and model merging as complementary approaches to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we combine these existing ideas into a simple retrieval-guided weight interpolation method. At each task, a lightweight retrieval module selects the most relevant previously trained adapters based on the current task’s features; the selected adapters are then merged with the newly trained adapter via weight averaging. This extends standard model merging by conditioning the interpolation weights on task similarity, and extends adapter routing by incorporating parameter-level knowledge. We evaluate our method in a limited setting: four tasks from Split-CIFAR-100 with a synthetic covariate shift, comparing against a single baseline of naive weight averaging. We do not include an ablation of the retrieval module or comparisons to more recent continual learning methods. Initial results suggest that retrieval-guided interpolation can reduce forgetting by a small margin on two of the four tasks, while performing on par with the baseline on the others. Overall, the contribution is incremental and would benefit from a larger-scale study; nonetheless, the combination of retrieval and merging appears promising for further investigation.

title: Preliminary Application of World-Model-Augmented Web Agents to Organic Afterglow Literature Mining
abstract: We apply the world-model-augmented web agent with action correction, an existing framework, to the task of retrieving and summarizing synthesis recipes from the organic afterglow materials literature. As a preliminary exploration, we curate a small dataset of 30 recent papers from this domain and run the agent in its default configuration. We report initial results: the agent successfully identifies key synthesis parameters in 60% of cases, but fails to correct action errors in the remaining cases. However, we do not compare against any baseline systems, and the dataset is too small to draw general conclusions. Our work is a straightforward application with no methodological novelty; we simply transfer the framework to a new domain. We also observe that the agent's internal world model, trained on general web data, lacks domain-specific knowledge, leading to suboptimal search strategies. Nevertheless, these initial experiments suggest that further domain adaptation and a larger evaluation corpus are necessary before any claims about applicability can be made. We hope this study can serve as a starting point for future work on using deep research agents in molecular informatics.

title: Applying Query2Label to Robotic Object Tagging: A Preliminary Study on a Small Custom Dataset
abstract: In this paper, we apply the Query2Label transformer framework, originally proposed for multi-label image classification, to the new domain of robotic object tagging. We collect a single small dataset of 120 images from a fixed camera overlooking a tabletop robot workspace, and manually annotate the presence of 10 everyday objects. We fine-tune a pre-trained Query2Label model on this dataset and report initial results using F1 score and accuracy. We also explore how varying brightness levels affect tag prediction performance. Our experiments are preliminary: we do not compare against existing object detectors or classification baselines, and the dataset is limited in size, object variety, and scene diversity. These constraints clearly limit the generalizability of our findings. Despite these limitations, the qualitative and quantitative results suggest that transformer-based multi-label classification may be adaptable to robot perception tasks, but more extensive validation with larger datasets and baseline comparisons is necessary. This work is intended as an initial exploration rather than a definitive solution.

title: Applying a Discrete Speech-to-Speech Translation Model to Medical Consultations: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We present a preliminary study applying PolyVoice, an existing discrete speech-to-speech translation framework, to medical consultation dialogues. We directly use the pre-trained model without any architectural modifications or task-specific fine-tuning, evaluating its feasibility on a newly collected small dataset of 40 simulated English-to-Spanish medical conversations, totaling 1.2 hours of speech. Our initial experiments measure translation quality using automatic metrics (ASR-based BLEU and a speech translation specific metric). The results indicate that the model produces partially intelligible translations but frequently omits critical medical terms. As a preliminary exploration, this study is limited by the small dataset size, the lack of baseline comparisons, and the absence of human expert evaluation. We also do not assess performance on other language pairs or in real clinical settings. These limitations make our findings primarily indicative of potential challenges and avenues for future research, rather than a validation of the approach. We hope this initial study encourages further work on adapting speech translation models to high-stakes domains like healthcare.

title: Applying Multi-LLM Ensemble Voting to Developer vs. LLM Code Classification: A Preliminary Study on a Small Dataset
abstract: We apply a multi-LLM collaboration method, originally developed for general reasoning tasks, to the problem of code evaluation. Specifically, we use an ensemble of three LLMs that independently score code snippets and then aggregate their outputs via majority voting to classify whether a code change was authored by a human developer or generated by an LLM. Our initial experiments are conducted on a single dataset of 120 code snippets extracted from a single GitHub repository. We report preliminary results showing that the ensemble achieves moderate accuracy, and we explore the effect of different prompt templates. We do not compare against any baseline methods, and we do not modify the underlying collaboration technique. The scope is limited: the dataset is small and domain-specific, the prompt templates are not optimized, and the results may not generalize to other repositories or code types. These limitations mean that our findings should be interpreted as an initial exploration rather than a validated solution. We conclude that applying this existing method to code evaluation yields mixed results, and further work with larger and more diverse datasets, as well as baseline comparisons, is necessary.

title: Applying ROME Knowledge Editing to Event Fact Correction: A Preliminary Study on a Small Political Dataset
abstract: Recent advances in knowledge editing have shown that large language models can be updated by directly modifying internal weights. In this paper, we apply an existing weight-based editing method, ROME, to a new domain: correcting factual event knowledge in a small corpus of political event descriptions. We explore whether this off-the-shelf method, originally designed for entity substitution, can be directly transferred to update event facts without any methodological changes. We conduct initial experiments on a single dataset of 250 event descriptions, reporting post-edit accuracy and consistency metrics. No baseline methods are included, and hyper-parameters are left at their default settings. Results show that ROME achieves reasonable accuracy on simple event edits, but its performance declines on multi-relational and temporal statements. We also observe that the method sometimes introduces unrelated factual changes, which limits its practical reliability. This study is a preliminary exploration of cross-domain knowledge editing; we explicitly do not propose new techniques. We discuss the limitations of the evaluation, including the small dataset size, lack of comparisons, and domain specificity, and suggest directions for future work. Overall, our findings indicate that existing editing methods may require domain-specific adaptation to be effective for event-centric knowledge.

title: Spatial Mask Consistency with World-Model-Inspired Perturbation for Semi-Supervised Left Atrium Segmentation
abstract: We propose an incremental extension of semi-supervised 3D left atrium segmentation by integrating a lightweight spatial reasoning module inspired by recent world models. Our method combines a cross-slice context consistency loss with a spatial mask prediction task, where input volumes are perturbed with frequency-domain masks and the model is trained to recover the original segmentation from a spatially transformed feature space. This mimics world-model-style self-supervision and encourages global anatomical structure learning. We evaluate the proposed approach on a single public left atrium dataset with only 10% labeled volumes, comparing against a standard mean-teacher baseline and a recent mask consistency method. In this limited setting, our method improves the Dice score by 1.3 points over the baseline, but gains are inconsistent across other metrics and no statistical significance is reported. We also provide qualitative visualizations, but no ablation of the spatial reasoning module is performed. These initial results suggest that integrating spatial reasoning into semi-supervised medical segmentation is promising, yet the contribution remains marginal and would require substantial additional experiments, multiple datasets, and thorough ablations to be fully validated. The work is a direct combination of existing ideas from spatial reasoning models and mask-based consistency, rather than a novel problem formulation.

title: Multi-Morbid Synthetic Patient Generation for Conversational Symptom Assessment: A Limited Feasibility Study
abstract: Recent work has shown the promise of synthetic patients for training and evaluating conversational symptom-assessment agents. However, existing synthetic user generators model single, isolated conditions, limiting their realism for primary care, where multi-morbidity is common. We present an incremental extension of the SyntheticUser framework that conditions patient profiles on co-occurring chronic conditions (e.g., diabetes and hypertension) using a rule-based comorbidity matrix combined with a prompted large language model. We generate a small corpus of 120 simulated primary-care dialogues and use it to fine-tune a lightweight dialogue triage model. In a limited evaluation against a single baseline (the original single-condition generator), our approach yields modest gains in differential-diagnosis coverage (F1 +3.1 points) but does not significantly improve patient satisfaction ratings. We conduct no ablations of the rule-based component, and we do not test on real patient data. Initial results suggest that multi-morbid synthetic patients may add realism for training conversational agents, but substantial validation and additional baselines are required before any clinical deployment.

title: FedMotionLM: Federated Motion Forecasting as Language Modeling with Adaptive Game-Theoretic Client Reweighting
abstract: We introduce FedMotionLM, a new federated learning framework that trains multi-agent motion forecasting models as sequence generators across distributed data silos without sharing raw trajectories. Unlike prior federated methods that treat clients equally or add uniform noise, FedMotionLM formalizes client participation as a network effects game, where each client's contribution is adaptively reweighted based on the marginal improvement of its local model to the global prediction skill. To safeguard trajectory privacy, we propose a novel adaptive differential privacy mechanism that allocates noise budget per client according to its data heterogeneity, yielding an average 2.3x lower privacy loss at equal utility. In experiments on three benchmarks, FedMotionLM establishes new state-of-the-art results: on Argoverse 2, it reduces minimum Average Displacement Error (minADE) from 0.61 to 0.56 and Miss Rate (MR) from 0.13 to 0.11; on NuScenes, minADE drops from 0.72 to 0.68; on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, MR improves from 0.17 to 0.15. In addition, on the CIFAR-10 and FEMNIST federated benchmarks, FedMotionLM improves accuracy from 84.3% to 85.7% and from 76.1% to 77.4%, respectively. Our work provides the first privacy-preserving federated framework for motion forecasting with game-theoretic client incentives and adaptive differential privacy.

title: Direct Application of a Multi-Modal Siamese Network to Few-Shot Event Relation Extraction in Scientific Abstracts
abstract: In this paper, we explore the direct application of a multi-modal Siamese network, originally proposed for few-shot knowledge graph completion, to the task of few-shot event relation extraction in scientific abstracts. We treat each event relation as a triplet analogous to a knowledge graph fact, and reuse the model's textual and structural encoders without architectural modifications. We evaluate the model on a single small dataset consisting of 200 human-annotated abstracts reporting NLP experiments, covering 10 event relation types with 5 support instances per type. Our initial experiments yield a macro-averaged F1 score of 58.2%, but we note that the dataset is small, the relation types are selected for convenience, and no baseline methods are included. The results are preliminary and should be interpreted with caution; they mainly demonstrate feasibility rather than effectiveness. Limitations include the lack of comparison to existing few-shot relation extraction or event extraction models, the narrow domain coverage, and the fact that the model's multi-modal components are not fully exploited since only text is used. Overall, this is an application-oriented exploration with no methodological novelty; we hope it serves as a starting point for future work that adapts knowledge graph completion techniques to event extraction in more realistic settings.

title: Spatial Memory Enhanced Masked Attention for Closed-Loop Instance Segmentation
abstract: We present an incremental extension of the Masked-Attention Mask Transformer (Mask2Former) by injecting a lightweight spatial memory module derived from a world model representation. The proposed method, SpatialMask, uses a frozen world model encoder to produce a spatial prior that conditions the masked attention mechanism for instance segmentation. This combination is natural because masked attention transformers and spatial world models both rely on structured latent representations. We evaluate SpatialMask in a limited closed-loop setting on a synthetic indoor navigation environment. We build on the Mask2Former architecture and replace its standard attention queries with spatially grounded queries sampled from the world model's latent space. The world model is pre-trained offline on a semantic segmentation task. Initial results suggest a modest improvement in segmentation quality for seen object categories, but the performance gain diminishes for unseen objects. We also observe that the spatial memory module degrades when the world model is not fine-tuned. Due to time constraints, we do not provide ablations on the memory injection location, nor do we compare with recent state-of-the-art segmentation models such as Mask DINO. Our analysis is restricted to one simulation environment with only 20 episodes and a single A100 GPU. These preliminary findings indicate that integrating spatial memory into masked attention is feasible but requires substantial further investigation to be practically useful. We plan to release code upon acceptance.

title: Applying a Target-Agnostic Gender-Aware Contrastive Objective to Reduce Gender Bias in Medical Machine Translation: A Preliminary Study on a Small Clinical Corpus
abstract: We apply a target-agnostic gender-aware contrastive learning objective, originally developed for multilingual machine translation, to reduce gender bias in medical translations. Our domain is a small parallel corpus of clinical discharge summaries (English-Spanish) that we constructed from public sources. We fine-tune a pretrained multilingual MT model with the contrastive objective and report preliminary results. On our corpus, the approach reduces masculine default translations by about 15% for female patient references while preserving BLEU within 1 point of the fine-tuned baseline. However, we do not compare against any other debiasing methods, and our evaluation is limited to a single small dataset of 2,000 sentences. We also find that the objective is sensitive to hyperparameters and shows inconsistent gains across medical subdomains, suggesting limited generalizability. These initial experiments are exploratory; we do not claim any methodological novelty, and we expect that larger, annotated clinical corpora and additional baselines are needed to validate the approach. Our findings indicate that existing debiasing techniques may transfer to medical translation, but should be adapted and evaluated more rigorously.

title: Temporal Graph Clustering for Interaction-Aware Motion Forecasting: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We present an incremental extension of [profile-derived reference removed] to multi-agent motion forecasting. Our method, TC-MAF, applies a contrastive temporal graph clustering objective to group agents with similar interaction patterns over time, and then uses the resulting cluster assignments as auxiliary features in an attention-based forecasting backbone. This is a direct combination of existing ideas from graph clustering (Dink-Net) and motion forecasting (Wayformer), with no new architectural components. We evaluate TC-MAF in a limited setting on a single dataset, the Interaction dataset, against a small set of baselines. In this setup, initial results suggest that the cluster features yield a slight improvement in prediction accuracy for a subset of scenario types, but the gains are inconsistent across evaluation metrics and are not statistically significant compared to the baseline. We do not include ablations of the clustering components or test on additional datasets, and we defer these analyses to future work. Overall, the contribution is marginal: our findings indicate potential for combining temporal graph clustering with motion forecasting, but substantial revision is required to establish clear and consistent benefits over existing methods.

title: RoutEQA: Difficulty-Aware Routing for Cost-Effective Question Answering with Heterogeneous LLMs
abstract: We introduce RoutEQA, a difficulty-aware routing framework for question answering (QA) that allocates queries to heterogeneous LLMs based on estimated reasoning complexity. Unlike prior routing methods that rely on logit-based confidence or fixed thresholds, RoutEQA learns a lightweight difficulty probe on top of frozen sentence-level embeddings from a small encoder, trained with a pairwise rank loss augmented by on-policy synthetic query generation. At inference, the probe outputs a complexity score, and a dynamic programming policy selects a model from a given ensemble to balance accuracy and total cost. On three QA benchmarks (GQA, HotpotQA, and StrategyQA), RoutEQA improves accuracy by up to 6.2 points over a strong single-model baseline while reducing inference cost by 41% on average, and outperforms existing routers such as FrugalGPT and RouteLLM by 3–5 points at matched cost. Ablations confirm that the on-policy augmentation and pairwise ranking both contribute to the gains. We also analyze failure cases on multi-hop and adversarially rephrased questions, identifying a robustness gap that we discuss as a limitation. Our code and data will be released.

title: Applying Genetic Programming-Based Feature Extraction to Medical Text Classification: A Preliminary Study
abstract: In this paper, we apply a genetic programming-based feature extraction method, originally developed for binary image classification, to the task of medical text classification. Our goal is to explore whether this evolutionary approach can be directly transferred to textual data without modification. We use a small dataset of 500 clinical discharge summaries labeled for the presence of pneumonia, and we extract text features via n-grams and word embeddings, which are then fed into the GP system to evolve a feature set for a logistic regression classifier. Initial experiments show that the evolved features achieve an accuracy of 82% on a held-out test set. We do not compare against traditional feature selection methods or modern neural baselines, and we acknowledge that the dataset is small and the text preprocessing is minimal. These preliminary results suggest that GP-based feature extraction may have some potential for textual data, but significant work is needed to validate the approach on larger, more diverse medical corpora. We also note that no methodological changes were made to the original GP algorithm, so the study is an exploratory application rather than a novel method.

title: Applying Diffusion Language Models to Multi-Label Tagging of Transmission Electron Microscopy Images: A Preliminary Study
abstract: This paper presents an initial exploration of applying a diffusion language model to multi-label tagging of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images. We combine a pre-trained vision transformer for image feature extraction with a diffusion-based text generation model operating on the extracted features to produce tag sequences. We evaluate the pipeline on a single small dataset of 900 TEM images collected from a single facility, with manual tags from one annotator. No baseline comparisons are performed; the aim is to assess feasibility of this straightforward application in a new domain. Initial experiments show that the diffusion model generates syntactically valid tag sequences, but the tag overlap with ground truth is low (F1 < 0.3), and the model frequently outputs generic terms. We identify several limitations, including the small dataset size, domain shift from natural images, and the simplistic conditioning mechanism. Overall, this work is a preliminary report and does not yet provide a usable tagging system for TEM images. We hope that these initial results will motivate further research with larger datasets and more sophisticated domain adaptation techniques.

title: Extending Sparse Embedding Modulation to Figure-Caption Retrieval in Host-Guest Materials Literature
abstract: Post-hoc debiasing of vision-language models has been proposed as a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for reducing harmful correlations in general-domain embeddings. In this paper, we investigate whether Sparse Embedding Modulation (SEM), originally introduced for general vision-language debiasing, can be extended to a specialized scientific domain with minimal modifications. We propose a straightforward extension that applies SEM to figure-caption retrieval over a small corpus of host-guest materials chemistry publications. The method keeps the underlying CLIP-style encoder frozen and modulates a sparse set of embedding dimensions using a projection trained on 150 in-domain figure-caption pairs. Initial results suggest the domain-adapted SEM improves recall@5 by 4% on the curated host-guest retrieval set compared to the standard SEM baseline, while maintaining accuracy on a general-domain benchmark. However, our evaluation is limited: the curated corpus contains only 200 figure-caption pairs and three chemical classes, and we do not include comparisons against full fine-tuning, LoRA, or strong prompt-engineering baselines. We also do not ablate the choice of sparse dimension count. Overall, these preliminary findings indicate that sparse post-hoc modulation is a promising but unproven approach for adapting multimodal embeddings to niche scientific literature; substantially larger evaluation is needed before drawing strong conclusions.

title: Transferring Universal Cell Embeddings to Colorectal Histopathology Patch Classification: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Universal Cell Embedding (UCE) is a foundation model for cell biology that maps cells into a shared representation space using large-scale single-cell data. In this work, we explore whether UCE features can be repurposed for histopathology image analysis, where tissue patches contain dense mixtures of cells. We propose a simple adaptation pipeline that splits each histopathology patch into smaller tiles, extracts UCE embeddings from each tile, and aggregates them by averaging before a linear classifier. The UCE backbone is kept frozen, and we only train the classification head. We evaluate on a single public dataset (Colorectal Cancer Tissue) restricted to six tissue types. Initial results indicate moderate classification accuracy, but we observe substantial confusion among classes with similar cellular composition. We note that no comparisons to ImageNet-initialized baselines or other medical imaging foundation models are made, and we do not ablate tile size, feature aggregation, or the effect of freezing different network layers. While the transfer is shown to be technically feasible, experiments are limited in scope and should be interpreted as preliminary. We believe this study is a first step toward understanding the reuse of cell-level foundation models in medical imaging, although substantial validation is required.

title: Cross-Graph: Cross-Component Graph Reasoning for Learned Image Compression
abstract: Learned image compression has recently benefited from cross-component priors that exploit redundancies among color channels. However, existing cross-component methods rely on fixed local or global priors that do not fully capture the structured dependencies between chroma and luma features. In this paper, we propose Cross-Graph, a learned image compression framework that formulates cross-component entropy modeling as a graph reasoning problem. We construct a graph whose nodes represent spatial positions in the latent space across the Y, Cb, and Cr channels, and whose edges encode both intra-channel spatial correlations and inter-channel dependencies. A graph attention network with multi-scale propagation is used to iteratively refine the latent representation and predict the entropy parameters for arithmetic coding. We further introduce a lightweight cross-component context module that anchors graph nodes to the most informative luma coordinates, improving compression efficiency without increasing bitrate. Experiments on the Kodak, Tecnick, and CLIC benchmarks show that Cross-Graph outperforms state-of-the-art learned codecs, including the recent local-to-global cross-component prior, achieving an average 5.2% bit-rate reduction at equivalent PSNR, and 4.1% reduction in MS-SSIM. The proposed method also demonstrates robust generalization to high-resolution images. A minor limitation is the increased decoding latency due to graph propagation, which we plan to address in future work.

title: Applying Causal Knowledge Graph Learning to Stress State Classification in IoT-Enabled DeFi Environments: A Preliminary Study
abstract: We explore the application of a causal knowledge graph learning method, originally developed for brain network analysis, to the new domain of stress state classification in IoT-enabled decentralized finance (DeFi) trading environments. Using a single small dataset collected from 14 participants during stressful and non-stressful simulated trading tasks, we construct subject-level graphs from electrodermal activity and heart rate variability features, and apply the existing Causal-KG framework to learn graph representations for binary stress classification. Our initial experiments report a mean accuracy of 68% on this dataset, with no baseline comparisons conducted. We also provide preliminary observations about the importance of specific physiological features, but these remain speculative and lack statistical validation. The work is a straightforward transfer of an existing method to a new domain, with no methodological novelty introduced. We explicitly acknowledge several limitations: the dataset is small and homogeneous, no cross-validation or significance testing is performed, hyperparameters are set heuristically, and the causal claims of the framework are not independently verified. We conclude that while the approach is feasible, the results are inconclusive and should be interpreted with caution. This is an initial exploration intended to highlight the potential of cross-domain graph learning, not a mature contribution.

title: Visual Context for N-ary Relational Link Prediction: Extending Relatedness Evaluation with CLIP Embeddings
abstract: [profile-derived reference removed] has largely focused on textual and structural features, while visual signals from associated images are rarely considered. We propose a simple extension of the relatedness evaluation framework for n-ary facts by incorporating visual context from entity images using a pre-trained CLIP model. Our method concatenates CLIP image embeddings with text-based relation embeddings and feeds them through a linear projection before scoring candidate facts. We evaluate on the Wiki People dataset using a single fixed split and compare only against the text-only baseline from the original relatedness model. In our limited experiments, visual context slightly improves link prediction for visually grounded relations such as profession but hurts performance on more abstract relations, yielding mixed overall results. We do not perform extensive hyperparameter tuning or include comparisons with recent strong baselines, and we only test one simple fusion strategy. Initial results suggest that visual context could offer marginal gains in specific settings, but substantial further investigation is required to determine its general utility. Overall, this work is an incremental extension of an existing scoring function, and the contribution is modest for the cross-modal AI and knowledge graph communities.

title: Heavy-FL: Joint Gradient Sketching and Client Selection for Asynchronous Federated Learning
abstract: We introduce the problem of joint gradient sketching and client selection for asynchronous federated learning under a stringent communication budget. We present Heavy-FL, the first framework that solves this problem by maintaining a count-min sketch of the smoothed gradient magnitudes across clients, simultaneously identifying (i) the top-k 'heavy-hitter' parameters that dominate the learning signal and (ii) the most informative clients whose local distributions deviate most from the global model. Heavy-FL transfers only heavy-hitter parameters from upweighted clients, and we prove it achieves the same order of convergence as full-precision FedAvg under bounded staleness. On CIFAR-10 with 100 clients and 1 Mbps wireless channels, Heavy-FL attains 94.2% top-1 accuracy, improving the prior state-of-the-art from 92.7% (async FedAvg) and 91.8% (FedProx), while reducing uplink traffic by 68.4%. On FEMNIST, it reaches 90.1% vs. 88.6% for FedAvg. On Stack Overflow Next Word Prediction, Heavy-FL cuts communication by 62.3% and achieves a perplexity of 44.1 (vs. 42.8 for full-communication FedOpt) in 1.7x less wall-clock time. These results establish Heavy-FL as the new state of the art for communication-starved asynchronous federated learning.
